ll174-the-levels-of-disrespect-and-the-g.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Does calling Yahweh's name carelessly matter more than you think? Yes. His name is His character, published by Himself: merciful, gracious, longsuffering, and exact about guilt. Disrespecting Him is not mispronouncing a word; it is saying something about Him that is not true. Even sincere people, defending Him, can do it without noticing, as Malachi's priests and Job's friends did. Here is how the Word shows the gap, and how it closes.
ll174-the-levels-of-disrespect-and-the-g.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Does it matter more than you think? It does, because every careless word about Yahweh either strips out His generosity, as the serpent did, or adds a fence He never built, as Eve did. Both make Him smaller than He is, and He told Job's friends, "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right" (Job 42:7). Sincerity was not the measure; accuracy was. So hear before you answer, search the Word daily, trust what He says of Himself, and stay near Him. The gap closes in His company.

teen.open: Does talking about Yahweh carelessly really matter? Yes. His name stands for who He is, so saying wrong things about Him is a big deal.
teen.close: So listen to what His Word actually says before you speak for Him. Spend time with Him, and you will get to know Him as He really is.

senior.open: We may think a careless word about Yahweh is a small thing. The Word teaches that His name is His character, so misstating Him is a real offence, even when done sincerely.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Speak of Yahweh only as He has spoken of Himself, test what you hear against the Word, and draw near to Him, for the gap between His meaning and our words closes in His presence.

ll175-true-love-starts-with-an-act-and-a.reason: Opens by listing Darrell's four claims but not why; the reasons (the deed is the proof, truth is the test's object, the heart cannot be read from inside) are spread across later sections. The ending lands well.
ll175-true-love-starts-with-an-act-and-a.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does love act first, test for truth, and never trust an unchecked heart? Because the Word defines love by deeds, not moods: suffering long and being kind come before any warmth (1 Corinthians 13:4). Because a test exists to find what is actually so, not to catch someone. And because the heart cannot read itself (Jeremiah 17:9), a feeling that comes before the test has nothing under it. Here is how the Word sets that order.
ll175-true-love-starts-with-an-act-and-a.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does love act first, test for truth, and never trust an unchecked heart? Love acts first because the deed is the love and the proof of it, as Jacob's seven years and Jesus' own words show (John 14:15). It tests for truth because love rejoices in the truth, and a test run to win has become a trap. It refuses the unchecked heart because no one can read that instrument from inside. Act, think soundly, prove the thing in meekness, and then the feeling rests on something real.

teen.open: Why should love act first and feel later? Because real love is something you do, and feelings can fool you until they are checked against what is true.
teen.close: So love starts with kind actions and clear thinking. You check what is true, gently and not to win. Then the feelings come, and they have something solid to stand on.

senior.open: The title asks why love acts before it feels. The Word answers plainly: love is defined by its deeds, a test exists to find the truth, and the heart cannot vouch for itself.
senior.close: So the order holds. Kindness aimed by a sound mind comes first, then a meek test whose only object is truth, and then the feeling. Affection that arrives in that order will still be standing next week.

ll176-faith-is-the-substance-and-the-evi.reason: Answers 'what faith is made of' early (substance and evidence, not a feeling), but the making-before-the-cross half arrives late, and the lesson ends on a THIS WEEK exercise list rather than the answer.
ll176-faith-is-the-substance-and-the-evi.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is faith a feeling? No. Hebrews 11:1 says faith is made of two hard things: substance, what a hope is built out of, and evidence, what stands up when a claim is challenged. And Yahweh's making comes before the cross because the One who made you on purpose is the same One who then died for you while you were still a sinner (Romans 5:8). Here is how the Word shows both.
ll176-faith-is-the-substance-and-the-evi.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Faith is not a feeling. It is the substance your hope is built from and the evidence that holds in a hearing, and it comes by hearing the Word (Romans 10:17). The making comes before the cross because it shows who is acting: the One who wrote your days before there were any (Psalm 139:16) is the One who died for you before you tidied up. Made first, then died for. That is why you want to please Him, and why not.

teen.open: Is faith just a feeling? Hebrews 11:1 says no. Faith is what your hope is made of, and it is real evidence. And the One who made you is the One who died for you.
teen.close: So faith is not a mood. It is solid, and it comes from hearing the Word. Yahweh made you on purpose, then Jesus died for you. Why would you not want to please Him?

senior.open: The title asks whether faith is a feeling. Hebrews 11:1 names it substance and evidence instead, and the order of Yahweh's acts, making us and then dying for us, shows why we answer Him.
senior.close: So faith is the material a hope is built from and the evidence it rests on. And because the One who made you deliberately is the One who died for you while you were yet a sinner, pleasing Him is the only reasonable answer.

ll177-two-minds-and-the-one-you-feed-is-.reason: Directive names two minds and capture-test steps, but never says plainly which mind is driving; that answer (the one you feed and live out of; unwatched thoughts run you) is spread across a long lesson ending on an exercise list.
ll177-two-minds-and-the-one-you-feed-is-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Which mind is driving your decisions? Whichever one you feed and live out of. Everyone carries two, the carnal mind and the spiritual mind (Romans 8:5-6), and if you never watch a thought, it goes straight from arriving to acting with the carnal mind at the wheel. The way to watch is to switch on the observing layer: capture the thought, test it against the Word, act on what the Word says, and keep what proves good. Here is how the Word lays that out.
ll177-two-minds-and-the-one-you-feed-is-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Which mind is driving your decisions? The one you have been feeding. The carnal mind cannot be brought under His law (Romans 8:7), so the work is not repairing it but choosing which mind you live from. You watch a thought by capturing it in a sentence, running it through the eight filters of Philippians 4:8, acting on the Word once where it costs you, and writing down what happened. Keep the kind that bore fruit and cast down the rest, and ask Him to search you (Psalm 139:23). Then the spiritual mind is the one at the wheel.

teen.open: Which mind is making your choices? You have two, a spiritual mind and a carnal one. The one you feed is the one that runs you, unless you learn to stop and look at a thought first.
teen.close: So catch the thought, write it down, and check it against Philippians 4:8. Then do what the Word says and see what happens. Keep feeding that mind, and it will be the one driving.

senior.open: The title asks which mind is driving your decisions. Scripture names two, the carnal and the spiritual, and the answer is whichever one you feed. A thought never observed is acted on by default.
senior.close: So the spiritual mind drives when the observing layer is switched on: the thought captured, tested against the Word, acted on, and its result recorded. Invite Yahweh to do the searching with you, and the mind you feed becomes the mind that leads.

ll178-terms-change-not-the-need-a-rename.reason: Answers the 'why' early through James 2:15-16, but the 'how Yahweh measures' half (the real state, the deed, the fire that tries the work) is scattered, and the lesson ends on a THIS WEEK checklist.
ll178-terms-change-not-the-need-a-rename.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why can a kind sentence leave a need untouched? Because words can rename a problem without changing it. Saying "be ye warmed and filled" is true and kind, and the person is still cold and hungry when it ends (James 2:16). And how does Yahweh measure whether it was fixed? Not by the label or the intention, but by the real state on the ground, tested by what was actually done. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll178-terms-change-not-the-need-a-rename.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. A kind sentence can leave a need untouched because a new name is not a repair; it is healing the hurt slightly, saying peace when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Yahweh measures by the state, not the story: whether the person is clothed, whether the wall is finished with a date on it (Nehemiah 6:15), whether the work survives the fire that tries it of what sort it is (1 Corinthians 3:13). So check the state, do one thing that changes it, and love in deed and in truth. The need stands until it is fixed.

teen.open: Why can nice words leave a problem unfixed? Because giving a problem a new name does not change it. Yahweh looks at whether the need was actually met.
teen.close: So do not stop at kind words. Look at how things really are, then do something that changes it. A need is fixed when it is fixed, not when it is renamed.

senior.open: The title asks why a kind sentence can leave a need untouched. James answers it: words that rename a need without meeting it profit nothing, and Yahweh measures by the real condition, not the description.
senior.close: So the measure is the state itself. A renamed problem may satisfy an audience, but it does not satisfy the Judge. Know the true condition, change it in deed, and remember that the need stands until it is fixed.

ll179-heartfelt-the-heart-is-the-deep-mi.reason: Opening paragraphs say plainly that 'heart' is not feelings but the deep mind that runs you; the last lines land it: 'The heart is the deep mind. What is written there is what will come out of you.'

ll181-run-it-through-the-word-the-two-mi.reason: The answer (not on your own steadiness, but yes as a confession of Him who is able to keep you, Jude 1:24) arrives mid-lesson; the ending drifts to deception, wealth and no condemnation.
ll181-run-it-through-the-word-the-two-mi.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can you promise Yahweh what your flesh might not keep? Not as a boast about your own steadiness. The Word warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:5), and Peter meant his promise and broke it. But you can sing it honestly when it becomes a confession about His keeping: He works in you both the will and the doing (Philippians 2:13), and He is able to keep you from falling (Jude 1:24). Here is how one choir found that in the Word.
ll181-run-it-through-the-word-the-two-mi.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you promise Yahweh what your flesh might not keep? On the strength of your flesh, no; Romans 7:18 says plainly that the performing is not in you. On His strength, yes. The lyric became singable when it stopped leaning on her and started leaning on Him that is able to keep you from falling, the same Lord who prayed for Peter before Peter fell. Her hesitation was reverence, and the Word turned it into a song the whole room could sing gladly. Run the fearful thought through the Word, and sing what He will keep.

teen.open: Can you promise Yahweh something you might not be strong enough to keep? Not by bragging about yourself. But you can when you are leaning on Him to keep you.
teen.close: So you cannot promise on your own strength. Peter tried and fell. But Jude 1:24 says He is able to keep you from falling. Sing it about Him, and you can sing it honestly.

senior.open: The title asks whether we may promise Yahweh what our flesh might not keep. Scripture warns against vows made on our own steadiness, yet it gives us a promise we can rightly lean on: His keeping.
senior.close: So the answer is careful and glad at once. We do not vow on the strength of the flesh, which fails, as Peter learned. We confess the One who works both the will and the doing in us and is able to keep us from falling.

ll180-he-giveth-thee-power-to-get-wealth.reason: Opens well on 'power to get, not wealth', but what wealth is meant to serve (establishing His covenant) appears only in the last short section, and why the waiting persists (a Knowledge gap) is mid-lesson.

What usually holds people back is not permission but a gap in Knowledge, which you are told to go and get. And the wealth has a job: that He may establish His covenant. Here is how the verse shows it.
ll180-he-giveth-thee-power-to-get-wealth.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. If you hold Deuteronomy 8:18 and are still waiting, the verse is not late; it has already handed you the power. And keep the wealth pointed at its job, establishing His covenant, asked for with "If the Lord will" rather than assumed.

teen.open: Still waiting for Yahweh to make you rich? Deuteronomy 8:18 says He already gave you the power to get wealth. Now you use it.
teen.close: So do not just wait. Learn what you are missing, start with what you know, and give Him the credit. The wealth is for His covenant, not just for you.

senior.open: The title asks why someone handed the power could still be waiting. Deuteronomy 8:18 gives a capacity, not a delivery, and it names the purpose: that He may establish His covenant.
senior.close: So the gift is already given. What remains is our part: to act on what we know, to acquire the Knowledge we lack, to credit Him for the power, and to let the wealth serve His covenant, Yahweh willing.

ll182-two-witnesses-jesus-counted-them-h.reason: Opens on Darrell's test (let the Word explain the Word); what happens when Jesus tests His claim (He counts Himself and the Father as two witnesses, John 8:18) comes mid-lesson; ends on how to carry it gently.
ll182-two-witnesses-jesus-counted-them-h.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What happens when Jesus puts His own claim to the test? He meets the Law's own standard. Two who bear witness, the Sender and the Sent, and His claim stands. Here is how the Word shows it, with nothing but the Word.
ll182-two-witnesses-jesus-counted-them-h.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. When Jesus put His own claim to the test, He did not exempt Himself. He submitted to the rule of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), counted Himself as one and the Father as the other, and the claim held. Read John 5:31, then Deuteronomy 19:15, then John 8:17-18, and let the Word explain the Word.

teen.open: What happens when Jesus tests His own claim? He follows the rule that two witnesses are needed, and He counts them: Himself and the Father.
teen.close: So Jesus passed His own test. Two witnesses, the Father and the Son, and the claim stands. You do not need a debate, just the verses, read in order.

senior.open: The title asks what happens when Jesus submits His own claim to the Law. He cites the rule of two witnesses and counts Himself and the Father as the two.
senior.close: So His claim stands by the very standard He quoted: the Sender and the Sent bear witness together, one LORD, never at odds. The passage does its own work when we let the Word explain the Word.

ll183-realign-my-eyes-your-type-was-trai.reason: Opens on 'your type was trained', but what Jacob, Jonathan and Job each teach is spread through a very long lesson; the 'short version' ending lands the retraining but never ties the three men together.
ll183-realign-my-eyes-your-type-was-trai.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If a feed trained your eyes, how does Yahweh retrain them, and what do Jacob, Jonathan and Job teach about seeing people clearly? Your type was taught one scroll-stop at a time, and it can be retaught. Jacob is the warning: his eye ranked two sisters, and Yahweh honoured the one he passed over. Jonathan is the measure: kindness that costs. Job is the method: a covenant made with your eyes in advance. Here is how the Word lays it out.
ll183-realign-my-eyes-your-type-was-trai.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your eyes were trained by what you fed them, and the One who made them can retrain them. Jacob shows that a choice made by the eye can be sincere and still wrong, and that Yahweh builds through the person the eye ranked last. Jonathan shows what to measure instead: kindness that costs the one showing it. Job shows how to guard the intake, by deciding in advance what your eyes will dwell on (Job 31:1). Purge the feed, cast the images down when they return, ask Him to realign your eyes, and then you see the whole person.

teen.open: What you scroll past and stop on trains what you find attractive. The good news is that Yahweh can retrain your eyes, and Jacob, Jonathan and Job show how.
teen.close: So clean up your feed and make a promise with your eyes, like Job did. Look for kindness that costs something, like Jonathan's. And ask Yahweh to help you see people the way He does.

senior.open: The title promises that eyes trained by a feed can be retrained. Jacob warns what the ranking eye costs, Jonathan shows what to weigh instead, and Job shows how to guard the intake.
senior.close: So the retraining is real and it takes time. Guard the intake as Job did, weigh costly kindness as Jonathan showed, remember that Yahweh honoured Leah, and ask Him to bring your eyes back into calibration.

ll184-he-sings-yahweh-over-you-jesus-in-.reason: Opens by saying plainly that Yahweh and Jesus sing and Zephaniah 3:17 follows at once; the closing section ('Why this makes you know Him better') lands the answer: He sings over you, so He is glad about you, not enduring you.

ll185-knowledge-was-never-the-savior.reason: First paragraph answers it (Knowledge is supply from Yahweh, never the savior; supply versus source), and the last paragraph lands it: keep the arrow pointed down, He gives Knowledge, neither was ever the savior.

ll186-glory-to-glory-one-letter-holds-bo.reason: Opening says yes, the Word clears it up: one letter holds both claims. 'The short version' ending lands it: verdict settled, process ongoing, finishing His; not arrived, not abandoned, being changed.

ll187-the-unreasonable-standard-and-the-.reason: Opens describing the gaokao method; the 'take the method, not the grinding' answer comes in section two, but the 'serve Yahweh' half (our reason for learning is Yahweh; the reward is Him) arrives only near the end of a very long lesson.
ll187-the-unreasonable-standard-and-the-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can a demanding study method serve Yahweh without crushing the learner? Yes, if you take the method and refuse the grinding. Set a specific standard, count its cost before you start, study by recall, and keep an honest log of your mistakes. But rest is His law, not a prize for the productive (Mark 2:27), and the reason for learning is Yahweh Himself, not the gate. Here is how the Word backs each move.
ll187-the-unreasonable-standard-and-the-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. A demanding method serves Yahweh when it is aimed at Him and kept inside His limits. Every move in it already had a verse under it: no beating the air, the counted cost of the tower, precept upon precept, the Word hid in the heart, the just man who falls seven times and rises. What keeps it from crushing anyone is the sabbath kept in it and the right Examiner over it: study to shew yourself approved unto Him (2 Timothy 2:15), and know that the reward is Him. Aim hard, count the cost, then stop and rest.

teen.open: Can you study really hard and still honor Yahweh without burning out? Yes. Use a strong plan, but keep the rest He built into the week.
teen.close: So aim high, plan for the cost, and learn from every mistake. But take your sabbath, and remember why you study: for Yahweh, not just the test. He is the real reward.

senior.open: The title asks whether a rigorous study method can serve Yahweh without crushing the one who learns. The lesson's answer is yes: take the method, refuse the grinding, and study toward Him.
senior.close: So the rigour is welcome and the rest is required. A specific standard, an honest error log and a counted cost are all scriptural, and the sabbath and the true Examiner keep them in their place. The aim is to know Him.

ll188-the-acceptable-year-and-the-whole-.reason: Opens on Darrell's shouts and the Luke 4 scene; the definition of the acceptable year (the jubile of Leviticus 25, begun on the day of atonement) and why the rest of the scroll matters arrive in later sections.
ll188-the-acceptable-year-and-the-whole-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What was the acceptable year, and why did the rest of the scroll matter? The acceptable year is the jubile of Leviticus 25: liberty proclaimed to all, land and people returned home, trumpeted on the day of atonement. Jesus stopped before "the day of vengeance of our God" because only the first part had arrived, yet He handed the scroll back whole. Announcing timing is His authority; cutting the text out is theft. Here is how the Word shows both.
ll188-the-acceptable-year-and-the-whole-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. The acceptable year is Yahweh's own release: liberty for all, debts and land returned, beginning on the day the blood is applied (Leviticus 25:9). Jesus declared it fulfilled and stopped mid-verse because the day of vengeance had not come, not because it was unwritten. The rest of the scroll matters because the whole counsel is His, and a Bible cut down to suit one group, whether in 1807 or by our own unnoticed habit, becomes a tool against the people it was given to free. Read to the end of the sentence.

teen.open: When Jesus read Isaiah in the synagogue, He stopped halfway through a verse. The acceptable year means Yahweh's year of freedom, when debts were released and people went home.
teen.close: So Jesus announced the freedom year had arrived, but He did not tear out the rest. Always read the whole passage, not just the parts you like. The whole Word belongs to Yahweh.

senior.open: The title asks what the acceptable year was and why Jesus stopped mid-verse. It is the jubile of Leviticus 25, and He stopped because only that part had come, while leaving the scroll whole.
senior.close: So the acceptable year is Yahweh's release, grounded in atonement, and the rest of the scroll stands because His counsel is whole. Reading every passage to its end is how we keep from the selective editing that once served injustice.

ll190-were-the-parables-real-the-one-who.reason: Opens answering Darrell's original 'were they real' question; why they still find you (their truth is aimed at the hearer, as with Nathan and David) is mid-lesson. The ending lands it well.
ll190-were-the-parables-real-the-one-who.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If some of Jesus' stories never happened, why do they still find you? Because a parable's truth was never in its characters; it is aimed at the hearer. Nathan's rich man never lived, yet David's verdict on himself was real. And the One who told the parables made the ages (Hebrews 1:2), so what He said holds in every age, including yours. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll190-were-the-parables-real-the-one-who.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. The parables still find you because they were made to. Like Nathan's lamb, they put a true picture in front of you and wait for you to see yourself in it. And the Teller is not a man inside one age reporting on another; He is the Son by whom the ages were made, the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). Whether the farmer stood in one field or none, the question is for you: which soil, which son, which man on the road? Answer it honestly, as David did.

teen.open: Some of Jesus' stories were made-up examples, so why do they still hit home? Because they are aimed at you, the listener, and Jesus made every age.
teen.close: So the point was never whether the farmer was real. The story is asking about you. Pick one parable this week and ask which person in it you are.

senior.open: The title asks why stories that may never have happened still reach us. The answer is in the form itself: a parable's truth is aimed at the hearer, and its Teller made the ages.
senior.close: So the parables find us because they were designed to, by the One who stands over every age. Nathan's story was for David; these are for you. Let one of them put its question to you, and answer it plainly.

ll189-follow-the-leader-the-shepherd-of-.reason: Never asks who you already follow; the answer (a camp, a hometown verdict, a rigged system, a father handed to you, unless you choose the Shepherd daily) is implied late in the heaven-on-earth section, then the close lists all of it.
ll189-follow-the-leader-the-shepherd-of-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who are you already following? Everyone follows someone. If you have not chosen the Shepherd on purpose, you are following whatever you were handed: a camp, your hometown's opinion of you, a system that profits from the dark, the father you inherited rather than the One you chose. The lesson shows the Leader worth following, Jesus, the Shepherd of your soul, who walked into rejection, suffering and the cross on purpose, for you.
ll189-follow-the-leader-the-shepherd-of-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who are you already following? The lesson leaves only two answers. Either the voices you were handed, the camp, the crowd, the comfortable arrangement with its two sets of scales, or the Shepherd who knows your name, laid His life down of Himself, and carries the government on His shoulder. It is a real choice and it is made daily (John 8:44). Choose Him, and following stops being a price: it is your answer to the One who first loved you (1 John 4:19).

teen.open: Everybody follows somebody, whether they picked them or not. The question is whether you are following Jesus, the Shepherd who chose the cross for you, or just whatever you were handed.
teen.close: So who are you following? If you did not choose, you are following the crowd. Jesus says "Follow me" and He already gave His life for you. Choose Him, every day.

senior.open: The title asks who you are already following, and the honest answer for most of us is: more than we realize. Habits, a camp, a town's opinion, inherited narratives. This lesson sets beside them the Shepherd of your soul, who walked into rejection and the cross on purpose.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. You are following either what you were handed or the Shepherd you chose, and the choice is made daily. He laid His life down first; following Him is the answer to that Love, not its price.

ll191-who-he-said-he-was-every-hearer-ev.reason: The yes (each hearer told in words he could bear) is in the opening, but the title's second half, what the key is and what it opens, only arrives after the sixteenth hearer; the ending turns to the reader without restating the keys plainly.
ll191-who-he-said-he-was-every-hearer-ev.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did Jesus tell each person who He was? Yes. He made no single speech about Himself; He told sixteen distinct hearers, friend and enemy, in the words each one's situation could hold, and they understood Him to claim what only Yahweh can claim. And the key in the title is His settled authority over the doors of death and the grave, won by going through them and rising. Here is the record, hearer by hearer.
ll191-who-he-said-he-was-every-hearer-ev.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did Jesus tell each person who He was? He did: the King of Israel to Nathanael, "I that speak unto thee am he" to the woman at the well, the resurrection and the life to Martha, "I am" to the council, a King with a kingdom not from here to Pilate. And to John on Patmos He named the key: He was dead, He is alive for evermore, and He holds the keys of hell and of death (Revelation 1:18). He opens what no one shuts. The first lock it opens is the fear of death in you (Hebrews 2:15).

teen.open: Did Jesus tell people who He really was? Yes, again and again, to sixteen different people in the Gospels and Revelation, each in the words they needed. And He says He holds the keys to death itself.
teen.close: So yes, He told each person who He was, in a way they could take in. He went through death and came back, so He holds its keys. That means you do not have to live afraid of dying.

senior.open: The title asks whether Jesus told each person who He was. The record says yes: to sixteen hearers, in words fitted to each situation, and every one understood Him to claim what belongs to Yahweh alone, ending with the keys of hell and of death.
senior.close: So the question is answered. He told each hearer who He was, whole, in the shape their situation could hold. He holds the keys because He passed through death and rose, and what He opens no one can shut. The first thing those keys release is the fear of death itself.

ll192-two-hours-became-six-the-pattern-t.reason: Opening states the question and lists five words (pattern, yea, inspection, settlement, faithful man) but gives no answer; the how only comes together in the final THE CLOSE summary, which lands well.
ll192-two-hours-became-six-the-pattern-t.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How do you build with someone who did not build what was agreed? You hold the pattern and you hold the man, both at once. Go to him alone, name the miss plainly and kindly against what four people heard him agree to, and ask him to make it right. Pay for what matched and only for what matched. Then hand the next job to faithfulness, and inspect from the first hour. Here is how the Word builds it.
ll192-two-hours-became-six-the-pattern-t.example: HOUR ONE, NOT HOUR SIX. Say the next job is specified the same way: this piece here, because it covers that one. This time you look at the first piece placed, against the pattern, before the second is started. If it is off, it costs a few minutes and one plain sentence. Left alone, the same drift becomes four parts in ten of a job by hour six. The lesson's point is simple: "The first hour tells you the sixth."
ll192-two-hours-became-six-the-pattern-t.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How do you build with someone who did not build what was agreed? The way Yahweh builds with us. He gives a pattern, He holds a yea as a vow, He looks upon all the work, and when it matches He blesses it. So you correct the man as a brother, not an enemy, pay justly in both directions, check your own beam, and give the next job to the one found faithful. That is how you edify and refuse in the same breath (1 Thessalonians 5:14).

teen.open: What do you do when someone says yes to a clear plan and then builds something else? You tell them straight and kindly, you check the work early, and you trust the next job to someone who keeps their word.
teen.close: So how do you work with someone who missed the plan? Talk to them alone, be honest and kind, pay what is fair, and check the work from the start next time. You can still want them to grow.

senior.open: The title asks how to keep building with someone who did not build what was agreed. The Word's answer is to hold both the standard and the person: a plain, private correction, a just settlement, and the next task given to faithfulness.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. Give a clear pattern, treat a yes as a vow, inspect early, settle justly both ways, and admonish as a brother rather than an enemy. That is how Yahweh builds with us, and it ends in "Well done, thou good and faithful servant" (Matthew 25:21).

ll194-i-am-who-he-said-he-was-every-hear.reason: Opening explains the counting rule and exclusions; the answer (58 occasions, each hearer given the whole truth in the shape he could carry) is stated only in WHAT THE FIFTY-EIGHT SHOW, then three further movements follow before the ending returns to it.
ll194-i-am-who-he-said-he-was-every-hear.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who heard Jesus say who He was, and what could each one bear? By a counting rule written down in the open, the four Gospels record fifty-eight scenes, from a twelve-year-old naming His Father in the temple to the eleven on the mountain in Galilee. He never gave one speech about Himself. Every hearer got the truth, whole, in the shape that hearer could carry. Here are all fifty-eight, in order.
ll194-i-am-who-he-said-he-was-every-hear.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who heard Jesus say who He was, and what could each one bear? Fifty-eight hearers in the Gospels, counted by one rule. He named Himself in thirty-eight scenes, received or corrected a confession in eighteen, answered a direct question in eight, and silenced spirits in four. A woman at a well heard it plainly, a council heard "I am" under oath, a grieving sister heard resurrection, a dying thief heard today. He has already said who He is to your situation too, and it is on the page.

teen.open: How many times did Jesus tell someone who He was? The four Gospels record fifty-eight scenes. Each person heard the full truth, but in a way they could handle right then.
teen.close: So, fifty-eight scenes, fifty-eight times the truth was told in a way the hearer could take in. He talks to your situation the same way. It is all written down for you.

senior.open: The title promises every person who heard Jesus say who He was. Counted by a rule stated in the open, the four Gospels give fifty-eight scenes, and in each one He told the hearer the whole truth in the form that hearer could bear.
senior.close: So the count stands at fifty-eight, each scene a different hearer and a different measure of what could be carried, yet always the same Christ. He has already spoken to your situation, and the Word keeps it for you to read.

ll193-what-it-costs-to-keep-your-soul-th.reason: Opens with a long summary of the Henrie interview; the answer (nothing is a fair exchange, yet souls are traded piece by piece for a morsel or applause, and sonship is what keeps it) is spread across later sections and gathered only in THE CLOSE.
ll193-what-it-costs-to-keep-your-soul-th.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What would you trade your soul for? Jesus already did the arithmetic: nothing in the whole world is a fair exchange (Mark 8:36-37). Yet souls are rarely lost in one dark moment. They are traded a piece at a time, for something small that looks huge on a hungry day: one morsel, or the applause of a room. What keeps you from the trade is knowing you are already a son or daughter of the Father. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll193-what-it-costs-to-keep-your-soul-th.example: THE BOWL ON A HUNGRY DAY. Say a salesman is told he can close the quarter if he says one untrue thing about the product. The commission feels like life that week, and his word feels like nothing. That is Esau's reasoning: I am about to die, so what good is a birthright? The lesson's answer is to refuse before the bowl, not after it. As it says, the same choice comes to a nurse, a salesman, a student and a pastor, not only an actor.
ll193-what-it-costs-to-keep-your-soul-th.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What would you trade your soul for? On a hungry day almost anything can look like enough: a bowl of stew, a role, the praise of men. Esau sold his birthright for one morsel. Jesus was offered every kingdom and the glory of them, and kept His worship for the Father alone. You keep yours the same way: settled as a son, trusting Yahweh over the fear of man, saying no at a price, standing among brothers. The honest answer is nothing. Your soul is not for sale, and keeping it is worth it.

teen.open: What would you trade your soul for? Most people do not sell it all at once. They trade it bit by bit for something small that feels huge right then, like fitting in or getting liked.
teen.close: So what is your soul worth trading for? Nothing. Esau sold his for one bowl of stew. You are a child of the Father already, so you do not need the crowd's approval. Keep your soul.

senior.open: The title asks what you would trade your soul for. Jesus answered first: nothing in the world is a fair price. Yet it is usually traded slowly, a piece at a time, for a small thing that looks large in a moment of need or a season of applause.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer: nothing. Esau's one morsel shows how the trade happens; sonship, trust in Yahweh, faithful friends and a willingness to say no at a price show how it is refused. A soul kept that way is kept well.

ll195-how-yahweh-keeps-his-word-the-prom.reason: Opens on the debate summary and Yahweh's promise; the answer to the title (use one scale for every book, put the Bible on it first, and its open record of variants holds) arrives mid-lesson in ONE SCALE FOR EVERY BOOK and the Isaiah Scroll section.
ll195-how-yahweh-keeps-his-word-the-prom.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Would your test for Scripture hold up if the evidence were open? It holds only if you use one scale for every book. You may not demand early manuscripts for another book and accept a feeling for the Bible (Proverbs 20:10). Put the Bible on that scale first. Its variants are catalogued and printed in the open, and the earliest copies show the same book. Yahweh keeps His Word, so it does not need the evidence hidden.
ll195-how-yahweh-keeps-his-word-the-prom.example: ONE BOOK ON THE OPEN SCALE. The lesson's own test case is the Great Isaiah Scroll, found in 1947 at Qumran and dated to about the second century before Christ, roughly a thousand years older than the medieval copies that had been the oldest complete Isaiah known. Laid beside the later text, it differs in many small ways, mostly spelling and grammar, and it is plainly the same book. Its photographs are published so anyone can look. That is what an open record lets you do: check it yourself.
ll195-how-yahweh-keeps-his-word-the-prom.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Would your test for Scripture hold up if the evidence were open? It will if you keep one standard: the same weights for every book, the earliest witnesses weighed most, and the Bible's own variants laid on the table rather than hidden. The Word passes that test because Yahweh keeps it, as He did when a king burned the scroll and the words were written again. So test everything, start with your own Book, and then speak to your neighbor with grace and the record open.

teen.open: If you would ask hard questions about another religion's book, would you ask the same ones about the Bible? You should. One fair test for every book, and the Bible can handle it.
teen.close: So does your test hold up? Only if it is the same test for every book. The Bible's old copies and small differences are out in the open for anyone to check. Yahweh keeps His Word.

senior.open: The title asks whether your test for Scripture would hold if the evidence were laid open. The Word requires one honest scale for every book, and the Bible can be put on that scale first, because its manuscripts and variants are already public.
senior.close: So the question is answered. A test holds when it is the same test for every book, and the Bible stands under it with its record open, as the Isaiah Scroll shows. The Word endures because Yahweh keeps it, and that frees us to speak to our neighbors with grace.

ll196-i-am-what-the-rest-of-the-word-tel.reason: Opens on the counting rule; who else spoke for Him and that every voice agrees with His own is only summed up in WHAT THE REST SHOWS and THE COUNT, CHECKED near the very end, after hundreds of entries.
ll196-i-am-what-the-rest-of-the-word-tel.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who else spoke for Him? Nearly everyone. Angels before He was born, an old priest and a widow in the temple, wise men from the east, John at the Jordan, a Roman centurion at the cross, a governor's sign over His head, and even Judas, who called his own betrayal innocent blood. Then the apostles and the prophets. Counted by one rule, the Gospels hold ninety-four more occasions, and every voice agrees with His own.
ll196-i-am-what-the-rest-of-the-word-tel.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who else spoke for Him? Gabriel said He would be called "the Son of God" before He was born, and the centurion said "Truly this was the Son of God" when He died. John called Him the Lamb, and heaven sang Worthy is the Lamb. His enemies told the truth in spite of themselves: the title said King, and the mockers said He saved others. His works, His predictions, the apostles and the prophets all say the same. Ninety-four occasions in the Gospels, and the whole Word with them. Now you are asked to be a witness too (Acts 1:8).

teen.open: Who else said who Jesus is? Angels, shepherds, strangers, a Roman soldier, even His enemies and Judas. The Word records ninety-four of these moments in the Gospels alone.
teen.close: So who spoke for Him? Pretty much everyone, friend and enemy, and they all agree with what He said about Himself. Now it is your turn to tell someone who He is.

senior.open: The title asks who else spoke for Jesus. The answer is a great crowd: angels, prophets, strangers, enemies, a governor, a soldier and the betrayer himself, counted here by the same rule as before, ninety-four occasions in the Gospels and many more beyond.
senior.close: So the question is answered. Every witness, willing or not, said what He said of Himself, from the angel's word to Mary to the song around the throne. The Word now asks the same of us: that we be His witnesses.

ll197-think-soberly-overlooked-promoted-.reason: Opening restates Darrell's questions at length without answering; promotion-is-Yahweh's arrives in movement three, sober measure in one, the Tyre craftsmen in seven; the close is a compressed list rather than the answer to 'promoted by whom'.
ll197-think-soberly-overlooked-promoted-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Overlooked at work, promoted by whom? By Yahweh, not by the memory of the people around you. Joseph's butler used his gift and forgot him for two full years, with no malice at all, and still the door opened on the day Pharaoh had a need. So think of yourself soberly: not more highly than you ought, not falsely small, counting your gift as something received. And keep your hands faithful, as Tyre's craftsmen did, building where the work is given.
ll197-think-soberly-overlooked-promoted-.example: THREE COLUMNS. The lesson asks you to read the data set of your own life in three columns. Say you write them out. In the first, where your gift was used: the projects people called you in for. In the second, where you were passed over: the openings that went past you while others remembered you only when they needed you. In the third, what came to you anyway by His hand, that no person arranged. The third column is the one Joseph could only read from the end.
ll197-think-soberly-overlooked-promoted-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Overlooked at work, promoted by whom? The butler forgot, but Yahweh did not, and the king's heart was in His hand all along (Proverbs 21:1). Promotion comes from neither the east nor the west; He puts down one and sets up another (Psalm 75:6-7). So measure yourself soberly, gift included, without comparing. Be content and still enlarge your tent. Do the work with faithful hands, as the craftsmen of Tyre did for the house of Yahweh. Then humble yourself under His hand, and let Him lift you in due time (1 Peter 5:6).

teen.open: Ever feel like people only notice you when they need something? Joseph felt that too. The answer: your rise comes from Yahweh, not from whether people remember you.
teen.close: So who promotes you when you are overlooked? Yahweh does. Know your gifts honestly, do not compare, keep working faithfully, and trust His timing. Joseph waited two years, and then the door opened in one day.

senior.open: The title asks who promotes the person who is overlooked at work. The Word answers: Yahweh, who turns the hearts of kings. Joseph was forgotten by the butler he helped, yet raised in a single day when the need arrived.
senior.close: So the question has a plain answer. Promotion is His, in His time and for His purposes. Our part is a sober estimate of ourselves, contentment with room to enlarge, faithful hands at the work given us, and patience under His mighty hand.

ll198-the-goldilocks-zone-of-curiosity-w.reason: The puzzle half is answered in the article summary, but how Yahweh hides just enough only arrives in movement one after a long source-check section; the ending lands the gap as where He draws us near, without tying back to the puzzle.
ll198-the-goldilocks-zone-of-curiosity-w.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does a half-finished puzzle pull you in? Because you know enough to see what is missing, and not so much that nothing is left to find. Yahweh made you that way and uses it. He conceals a thing so that kings will search it out (Proverbs 25:2), He shows the rest line upon line, as you are able to bear it, and the treasure at the end of the search is not a fact but a Person. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll198-the-goldilocks-zone-of-curiosity-w.example: THE SIGN IN THE FIELD. The lesson's own picture is the twelve stones at the Jordan. They stood in an ordinary field and did not explain themselves. A child would walk past and ask, "What mean ye by these stones?" and the answer was ready: the waters were cut off before the ark. Yahweh set a visible gap where the question would rise, then gave the answer at the moment it was wanted. The same pattern works at a table, in a class or in a church.
ll198-the-goldilocks-zone-of-curiosity-w.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does a half-finished puzzle pull you in? Because a gap you can see is an invitation, and Yahweh is the One who sets it. He hides a thing so kings will search, shows enough to hold, and paces the rest as you can bear it, the way Jesus asked "What seek ye?" and then said come and see. Settle how much it matters, aim your seeking at Him, and the missing piece turns out to be Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid (Colossians 2:3).

teen.open: Why can you not walk away from a puzzle that is almost done? Because you can see what is missing. Yahweh hides some things on purpose so you will come looking, and He shows the rest step by step.
teen.close: So the almost-finished puzzle pulls you in because the gap invites you. Yahweh leaves gaps like that in His Word on purpose. Keep searching, and you will find Jesus at the end of it.

senior.open: The title asks why a half-finished puzzle draws us in. We are most curious when we know part and not all, and the Word shows Yahweh using that very design: He conceals some things for us to search out, and reveals the rest in measures we can bear.
senior.close: So the question is answered. The visible gap draws us because Yahweh made us to seek and set the gaps Himself. Seeking aimed at Him arrives, and what is found is not merely a fact but Christ, in whom the treasures are hidden.

ll201-how-long-before-it-came-david-the-.reason: Opens on how the dictation arrived and on method; the actual spans (about 1,000 years from David, about 700 from Isaiah, about 500 from Zechariah) only gather in section ten; the close is about faithfulness, not the years.
ll201-how-long-before-it-came-david-the-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How many years passed between a promise and its keeping? It depends on the promise, and the Word lets us count. From David to Jesus is about a thousand years. From Isaiah, Hosea and Micah, about seven hundred. From Jeremiah, about six hundred; from Daniel, about five hundred seventy; from Zechariah, about five hundred; from Malachi to John the Baptist, 457 to 488. Every span is worked out from the years on both ends. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll201-how-long-before-it-came-david-the-.example: ONE PROMISE, TWO ENDS. Take Micah 5:2, the promise that the Ruler would come out of Bethlehem. Micah spoke in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, about 750 to 686 BC. Jesus was born in Bethlehem about 6 to 4 BC. Subtract the near ends and the far ends, and the promise waited 680 to 746 years. When Herod asked where the Christ should be born, the scribes answered from Micah's page (Matthew 2:5). That is how each span in this lesson is counted: a dated promise, a dated keeping, and the years between.
ll201-how-long-before-it-came-david-the-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How many years between a promise and its fulfillment? About a thousand from David, about seven hundred from Isaiah, Hosea and Micah, about six hundred from Jeremiah, about five hundred seventy from Daniel, about five hundred from Zechariah, and 457 to 488 from Malachi to John. The promises were spoken across about 580 years, by many men, and every one that reaches the Messiah lands inside one life. The years are how long He was waited for, and not one promise fell (Joshua 21:45).

teen.open: How long did people wait for Yahweh's promises about Jesus to come true? Hundreds of years. From King David it was about a thousand years.
teen.close: So the answer is: a long time, but never too long. David's promise waited about a thousand years, Isaiah's about seven hundred, and every one came true in Jesus.

senior.open: The title asks how long a promise waited for its keeping. The Word lets us count it: about a thousand years from David, about seven hundred from Isaiah and Micah, about five hundred from Zechariah.
senior.close: So the question has its answer in years. The promises were spoken across centuries by many men, from David a thousand years before, and every one that reaches the Messiah was kept within one life, the life of Jesus.

ll202-prepared-before-the-position-homec.reason: Opens on how the class was recorded; the answer (Yahweh prepares you, often through those who came before, as Moses prepared Joshua) arrives in sections two and four; ends on how the lesson was built, not the answer.
ll202-prepared-before-the-position-homec.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who prepares you for the position you have not reached yet? Yahweh does, and He usually does it through people and seasons you do not recognize as training at the time. Joshua served beside Moses for years before he led, and the hand was laid on him in public before the office was his. The hard days, the small errands, and the people who came before you are all part of His preparing. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll202-prepared-before-the-position-homec.example: ONE ERRAND AT A TIME. Look at the order in Joshua's life. First, Moses sends him to fight Amalek, and he does as he is told (Exodus 17:10). Next, he goes up the mount as Moses's minister (Exodus 24:13). Then he stays in the tabernacle while Moses speaks with Yahweh (Exodus 33:11). Then he sees Moses under pressure at the golden calf. Only after all that does Moses lay hands on him before the whole congregation (Numbers 27:18-20). Each step looked like a single assignment. Together they were the preparation for the position.
ll202-prepared-before-the-position-homec.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who prepares you for the position you have not reached yet? Yahweh does, long before the interview. He used Moses to train Joshua, and He used people like Mary E. Gwin to open doors for others before their work began. So your failures, your errands and your service beside a leader are not wasted; they are His training. And the same Yahweh who prepared you calls you to prepare the next ones, with the promise that He will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

teen.open: Who gets you ready for a job or role you do not have yet? Yahweh does. He often uses the people around you and the small things you do now.
teen.close: So the answer is Yahweh. Joshua learned by serving Moses long before he led. The small tasks and the people who help you now are how He gets you ready.

senior.open: The title asks who prepares us for a position before we reach it. The lesson answers plainly: Yahweh does, through the seasons and the people He places in our path, as He prepared Joshua under Moses.
senior.close: So the answer is Yahweh, working long before the position comes. He trained Joshua by years of service beside Moses, and He uses those who came before us. Our part now is to prepare the way for those who come after.

ll199-faith-in-good-faith-no-false-witne.reason: Opens on a long account of the Big Think email; the answer (argue the real person: no false witness, hear his real question, then declare the Word) only begins in section one; the close lands it but on goals, not the title's choice.
ll199-faith-in-good-faith-no-false-witne.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Do you argue the cartoon or the real person? The Word says the real person, every time. Painting your neighbor's belief as something easier to knock down is bearing false witness (Exodus 20:16). So you hear his real question before you answer, describe him truthfully, and then declare the truth to him from the Word, with meekness. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll199-faith-in-good-faith-no-false-witne.example: ONE QUESTION, TWO ANSWERS. Say a coworker tells you faith in Yahweh is just believing in a man in the sky. The cartoon answer mocks him back, or argues against something he never said. The real answer first asks what he means and hears it out. Then it tells him truthfully what the Word teaches: that Yahweh is a Spirit (John 4:24), that heaven cannot contain Him (1 Kings 8:27), and that He made Himself known in the Son (John 1:18). No cartoon of him, and no cartoon of Yahweh.
ll199-faith-in-good-faith-no-false-witne.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Do you argue the cartoon or the real person? The real person. Like Paul on Mars' hill, you learn what your neighbor actually believes and say it accurately, the way Paul read their altars and quoted their poets. Then you do not stop there; you declare the Word, gently and plainly. A cartoon wins an argument and loses the man. The real person, truly heard, is the one Jesus came to seek and to save (Luke 19:10).

teen.open: When you disagree with someone, do you argue with what they really believe, or a silly version of it? The Word says always argue with the real person.
teen.close: So argue with the real person, not a cartoon. Listen first, describe what they believe honestly, then share the Word kindly. That is how you love someone you disagree with.

senior.open: The title asks whether we argue against a cartoon of our neighbor or against what he truly believes. The Word answers plainly: a cartoon is false witness, so we hear the real person first.
senior.close: So the answer is the real person. We hear his actual question, describe his view truthfully as Paul did in Athens, and then declare the Word with meekness. The aim was never to win a debate, but to reach the neighbor himself.

ll200-how-did-they-know-the-record-they-.reason: Opens on how the dictation was recovered; the answer (the Law, Prophets and Psalms read aloud every sabbath named the colt, Bethlehem and David's line) comes in sections one to five; the close answers how they knew, not the scrolls question.
ll200-how-did-they-know-the-record-they-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did Jesus' crowd have the Scriptures in hand? Yes, in the way that mattered most: the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms were read aloud in the synagogues every sabbath (Acts 15:21). That record named a Son of David (2 Samuel 7:12), a birth in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), and a King riding on a colt (Zechariah 9:9). They had heard those promises all their lives. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll200-how-did-they-know-the-record-they-.example: ONE QUESTION FROM HEROD. When the wise men came, Herod asked the chief priests and scribes where the Christ should be born. They did not guess or debate. They answered from the page: in Bethlehem of Judaea, "for thus it is written by the prophet" (Matthew 2:5), reading Micah 5:2. That is what having the record looked like. A question came, and the answer was already written down, centuries old, and known well enough to quote on the spot.
ll200-how-did-they-know-the-record-they-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did Jesus' crowd have the Scriptures in hand? They did. The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms were read to them every week, and those pages named the Son of David, the town of Bethlehem and the King on a colt. Some still missed Him, because hearing the scroll is not the same as seeing the Man; the Father, His works and the Holy Spirit opened eyes. We have the same Scriptures today, now with the Gospels that show them kept.

teen.open: Did the people around Jesus know what the Bible said about Him? Yes. The Scriptures were read out loud to them every week.
teen.close: So yes, they had the Word. It told them about the colt, Bethlehem and David's family line. Some still missed Jesus, but those whose eyes Yahweh opened saw that the promises were about Him.

senior.open: The title asks whether the crowds around Jesus had the Scriptures. They did: the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms were read aloud every sabbath, and those pages named the Son of David, Bethlehem and the colt.
senior.close: So the crowd had the record, heard every week of their lives. It pointed plainly to the Son of David, the birth at Bethlehem and the King on a colt. Those who came to see Him in it were given eyes to see by the Father and the Holy Spirit.

ll204-the-word-checks-every-teller-many-.reason: Opening paragraph answers plainly (the Word, sourced outside the teller, corrects every teller and counsellor, so we all agree with Him first); THE CLOSE lands it: check every teller by the Word, ourselves first.

ll205-talk-about-it-together-parents-chi.reason: Opening states the big idea (talk in every direction) but never answers the title's who; the people (children, parents, friends) come in sections two to four and Yahweh listening only in Malachi 3:16; ends on verses and a bare imperative.
ll205-talk-about-it-together-parents-chi.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who are you really talking to about Yahweh? The people closest to you: your children, your parents, your friends, at the table, on the road, at bedtime and in the morning (Deuteronomy 6:7). The Word was given to be talked about in every direction, not only taught one way. And when those who fear Him speak often one to another, Yahweh Himself listens and a book of remembrance is written before Him (Malachi 3:16). Here is how the Word shows it.
ll205-talk-about-it-together-parents-chi.example: ONE CAR RIDE. Say a mother drives her son to practice. Instead of the radio, she asks one open question: what did you see about Yahweh in today's lesson? She listens to the end before she answers. He asks her one back. She answers with one verse and a short story from her own life. That is Deuteronomy 6:7 on the way, a child who asks like Deuteronomy 6:20, and swift to hear, slow to speak (James 1:19). Ten minutes, two directions, and Yahweh hearkening.
ll205-talk-about-it-together-parents-chi.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who are you really talking to about Yahweh? Your children, who need you to make His truth known with your own mouth. Your parents, who need your questions, because the Word built its memorials to be asked about by children. Your friends, who sharpen you as iron sharpens iron. And Yahweh, who hearkens when you speak of Him and writes it down. That is why the table, the car and the friendship matter: they are where a family gets healthy together and sees that Yahweh has been right.

teen.open: Who should you be talking to about Yahweh? Your parents, your family and your friends, in normal moments like dinner and car rides. And Yahweh listens when you do.
teen.close: So talk about Yahweh with the people right around you. Ask your parents questions, tell a friend what you learned, and know that Yahweh hears every one of those talks.

senior.open: The title asks who we are really talking to about Yahweh. The Word answers: our children, our parents and our friends, in the ordinary hours of the day, and Yahweh Himself hears it (Malachi 3:16).
senior.close: So the answer is the people nearest us, in both directions, and Yahweh listening above them all. The table, the road and the friendship are where His Word is handed on, until every generation can say that Yahweh has been right.

ll203-the-whole-line-of-promise-every-pr.reason: Section one opens right after a short preamble with 'The plain answer': David was where the question started, not the promise, which began in Eden the day sin came in; THE CLOSE restates it: David did not come first.

ll206-kings-who-search-it-out-the-word-s.reason: Opens on Darrell's list of phrases; the answer (concealing is an invitation for kings to search out, and the revealed things are for us and our children) sits mid-section one; the close is a list of phrases, not the answer.
ll206-kings-who-search-it-out-the-word-s.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does Yahweh hide things on purpose? Not to keep them from you, but to invite you to search for them. The Word says it is His glory to conceal a matter and the honour of kings to search it out (Proverbs 25:2), and what He reveals belongs to us and to our children (Deuteronomy 29:29). The searching is how He makes kings: people who read His Word daily, grow without end, and know Him better each year. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll206-kings-who-search-it-out-the-word-s.example: ONE VERSE, SEARCHED OUT. Say you finish this lesson on Nehemiah 8:10, the joy of the LORD is your strength. You could stop there. Or you search it out: you read the verses before it and find the people wept when they understood the Word, then rejoiced because they had understood it (Nehemiah 8:8-12). Now you see that the joy came from understanding. One verse, followed back a few lines, opened something the quick reading missed. That is the king's exercise, and the hidden thing was there for you all along.
ll206-kings-who-search-it-out-the-word-s.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does Yahweh hide things on purpose? Because a hidden treasure is an invitation, and He is raising kings who come looking. The king in Israel copied the Word in his own hand and read it every day of his life (Deuteronomy 17:18-19), so that he would fear Yahweh, keep a humble heart, and reign long. So the concealing is His glory and your honour: every search sends you deeper into the Word, renews your mind, and grows you toward Him for ever. Open the book and search it out.

teen.open: Why does Yahweh hide some things? So you will go looking for them. Searching His Word is how He grows you, like a king learning to rule.
teen.close: So Yahweh hides things as an invitation, not to keep you out. When you search the Word for yourself, you find more, you grow stronger, and you get to know Him better.

senior.open: The title asks why Yahweh conceals things on purpose. The Word answers that the concealing is His glory and the searching is the honour of kings (Proverbs 25:2); it is an invitation, not a withholding.
senior.close: So Yahweh hides things that we might search them out, as Israel's kings were to read the Word daily all their lives. What He reveals belongs to us and our children, and the search itself keeps the mind growing toward Him for ever.

ll207-the-worker-is-worthy-the-broken-de.reason: Opens on the speaker's talk and wage statistics; the answer (Yahweh wrote the deal, hears the worker's cry, masters answer to a Master, the worker serves Christ) is gathered only near the end, then the lesson closes on Talk About It.
ll207-the-worker-is-worthy-the-broken-de.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Your boss broke the deal? Then know whose deal it was. Yahweh wrote it: honest work is paid justly and on time (Deuteronomy 24:15), and a worker is not sent away empty (Deuteronomy 15:13). He hears the cry of the worker whose wages are kept back (James 5:4), and every boss has a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1). Your part is to keep working as unto Christ and leave vengeance with Him. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll207-the-worker-is-worthy-the-broken-de.example: BRICKS WITHOUT STRAW, TODAY. Say a shop cuts its training, freezes wages, and keeps the same quota, then calls the crew lazy when they fall behind. The Word named that pattern in Egypt: remove the provision, keep the quota, blame the worker (Exodus 5:7-18). It also shows what to do with it. Yahweh heard Israel's cry by reason of their taskmasters (Exodus 3:7). So the worker brings the wrong to Him, keeps working heartily as to the Lord (Colossians 3:23), may be angry without sinning (Ephesians 4:26), and does not take vengeance into his own hands.
ll207-the-worker-is-worthy-the-broken-de.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your boss broke the deal? The Word says the deal was never only his to break. Yahweh wrote it, He saw Jacob's twenty years when Laban changed his wages ten times, and He heard Israel under Pharaoh's quota. He still hears the cry of the hireling, and the one who hires answers to a Master in heaven. So you work heartily as unto Christ, carry your complaint to Yahweh instead of your own vengeance, and rest in His promise: He will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

teen.open: What if a boss does not pay you fairly or breaks a promise? The Word says Yahweh made the rules for fair pay, He sees it, and the boss answers to Him.
teen.close: So if a boss breaks the deal, Yahweh sees it and hears you. Keep working honestly like you work for Jesus, tell Yahweh about it, and let Him handle the payback.

senior.open: The title asks what the Word says when an employer breaks the deal. It says the deal was Yahweh's from the start: fair wages paid on time, no worker sent away empty, and every master answerable to a Master in heaven.
senior.close: So the broken deal is seen and heard. Yahweh rebuked Laban and heard Israel in Egypt, and He hears the hireling still. The worker's part is to serve as unto Christ, be angry without sin, and leave the settling of accounts with Yahweh.

ll208-the-gift-does-not-expire-the-skill.reason: Opens on the certification notice; the plain answer (no, the gifts of Yahweh are without repentance, Romans 11:29; the paper only witnesses to the gift) is reached in section one's end and section six; ends on Talk About It.
ll208-the-gift-does-not-expire-the-skill.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Paper can expire, but can a gift from Yahweh? No. The Word says the gifts and calling of Yahweh are without repentance (Romans 11:29): He does not take back what He gives. Skill is His gift, as it was for Bezaleel, whom He filled with wisdom, understanding and knowledge (Exodus 31:3). A certificate is only a witness to that gift. It can carry a date; the gift never did. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll208-the-gift-does-not-expire-the-skill.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Paper can expire, but can a gift from Yahweh? It cannot. The skill came from Him before any paper was printed, so no printed date can remove it. The paper is a witness, and a witness must be true and weighed with one weight. Your approval is before Yahweh, shown in work done heartily as unto the Lord. So keep the skill sharp, keep your witness true, and read any notice in peace, because He does not change, and His greatest gift, His Son, has no expiry at all.

teen.open: A certificate can run out, but can a gift from Yahweh run out? No. The Word says He does not take back what He gives.
teen.close: So the paper can expire, but your skill is Yahweh's gift and He does not take it back. Keep practicing, stay honest, and do your work like you are doing it for Him.

senior.open: The title asks whether a gift from Yahweh can expire as a certificate does. The Word answers no: His gifts and calling are without repentance (Romans 11:29), and a certificate only bears witness to the skill He gave.
senior.close: So the gift does not expire. A certificate is a witness and must be true, but the skill was Yahweh's before the paper existed. Keep it sharp, keep every witness honest, and rest in the One who does not change.

ll209-the-step-and-the-wait-the-work-of-.reason: Opening only previews that the Word has answers; the plain answer (do the work and commit it, promotion is Yahweh's, the wait has commands) is summed up in section eight; the lesson ends on Talk About It, not the answer.
ll209-the-step-and-the-wait-the-work-of-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. You sent your application and now there is silence; what does the Word say? Three things. The work of your hands was yours to do well, and now you commit it to Yahweh (Proverbs 16:3). The promotion is His, not the desk your papers landed on (Psalms 75:6-7). And the wait belongs to Him and has commands in it: wait on Him, pray instead of fretting, cast your care on Him, and keep working where you are. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll209-the-step-and-the-wait-the-work-of-.example: DAY FOURTEEN. Say it has been two weeks since you hit send, and the only reply was that your application was received. The Word gives you work for today. Pray about it with thanksgiving instead of carrying the worry (Philippians 4:6). Ask for wisdom about whether to follow up (James 1:5); Joseph asked the butler to remember him, and the Word does not condemn it (Genesis 40:14). Then keep doing excellent work where you are, as Joseph did in the prison, and go to sleep knowing who turns the king's heart (Proverbs 21:1).
ll209-the-step-and-the-wait-the-work-of-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Sent your application and now silence? The silence is not a sign that Yahweh is idle. You did your part: you prepared the work of your hands honestly and handed it up. Promotion comes from Him alone, and the heart of whoever reads your papers is in His hand. Your part now is to wait on Him with courage, cast your care on Him because He cares for you, keep working, and settle the answer before it comes: His will be done. Then, yes or no, your thoughts are established and your strength is renewed.

teen.open: Applied for something and heard nothing back? The Word says do your best work, give it to Yahweh, and trust Him with the answer.
teen.close: So when it is quiet after you apply, Yahweh is still working. You did your part. Pray instead of worrying, keep doing good work, and trust Him with the yes or no.

senior.open: The title asks what Scripture says when an application meets only silence. It says the work of our hands is ours to do and commit, the promotion is Yahweh's alone (Psalms 75:6-7), and the wait belongs to Him.
senior.close: So the silence is a season with commands in it. Commit the work, trust Yahweh who promotes, wait on Him with courage, cast every care on Him, and keep working faithfully, as Joseph did, until His due time.

ll210-what-really-drives-innovation-know.reason: Opens on the retail newsletter and its three observations; the one-sentence test a builder should measure (who was built up, was the weakest fed or sheared) only arrives at the end of section ten.
ll210-what-really-drives-innovation-know.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What should a builder really measure before shipping anything? Not whether the thing is new, and not only whether people would miss it if it vanished. Measure whether anyone was built up while it was there, and whether the weakest person it touches is fed by it or fleeced by it. A feature people love can still fail that test, because appetite misses what harms it. Here is how the Word sets that standard.
ll210-what-really-drives-innovation-know.example: ONE FEATURE, TWO DIRECTIONS. Say a team learns that people buy more when a countdown clock sits on the checkout screen. Measured by appetite, it is their best feature. Now run the lesson's test. Was anyone built up by it? Did the person who could least afford a rushed choice get fed, or sheared? Is the clock an honest weight, or a pressure the house set for its own gain? The same behaviour data can feed the flock or fleece it. The question decides which.
ll210-what-really-drives-innovation-know.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What should a builder really measure before shipping anything? Him first, then the people. Know the flock thoroughly, because you answer for them, but do not let what they currently want set the standard. Ask whether the thing edifies, whether every weight it shows is honest, whether it lifts a burden or lays one on, and whether the least of these is served by it. Love is senior to Knowledge. A feature that passes that test is worth shipping, even if no one ever notices it.

teen.open: Your favourite feature might be the one hurting people most. So what should a builder check first? Whether it actually builds people up, especially the weakest one using it.
teen.close: So here is the test before you ship anything. If it vanished tomorrow, who was built up while it was here, and was the weakest person helped or used?

senior.open: A builder is tempted to measure what is newest or most popular. This lesson measures something older: whether a thing edifies the people it serves, beginning with the weakest among them.
senior.close: So the answer to the title is settled by the Word. Measure what builds people up, keep every weight honest, and judge a feature by how it treats the least of these, not by how well it sells.

ll213-a-snag-in-the-theory-what-the-repo.reason: Says it will refuse gloating and hedging, but where to stand (on Hebrews 11:3, not on the snag) and the three-tier skill are only spelled out in sections six and nine; ends on the family prompt.
ll213-a-snag-in-the-theory-what-the-repo.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Where do you stand when the evidence shifts? You stand where you stood before the report arrived: on the Word, which says the worlds were framed by Yahweh's word (Hebrews 11:3). Your footing never rested on a scientist's difficulty, so a snag does not prove your faith and a fix next year does not shake it. Then you read the report honestly, sorting it into what is established, what is honestly open, and where a claim reaches past its evidence.
ll213-a-snag-in-the-theory-what-the-repo.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Where do you stand when the evidence shifts? On the same ground as before the news came in. Yahweh made the heaven and the earth, and the One who framed the worlds is the Lamb who takes away sin. From there you can read any report without gloating and without fear: state plainly what is established, name narrowly what is open, and let the Word correct only the claim that outruns its evidence. Evidence moves. That ground does not move one inch.

teen.open: When science news seems to shake things up, where do you stand? On the Word. Yahweh made everything, and that never depended on any one theory being right or wrong.
teen.close: So when the evidence shifts, you stay put on the Word. Then sort the news calmly: what is proven, what is still open, and what is just a big claim.

senior.open: Reports about origins come and go, and some believers rise or fall with each one. This lesson teaches a steadier place to stand: the Word first, then an honest sorting of the report.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. When the evidence shifts, we stand on Hebrews 11:3, as we always did, and we weigh every report fairly, granting what is established and correcting only what reaches past its evidence.

ll214-sons-of-yahweh-whom-he-made-whom-h.reason: Opening names made, begotten, adopted, but why we are adopted when angels are sons (He took our nature, made in His image) only arrives in section four; the summary lands in section ten.
ll214-sons-of-yahweh-whom-he-made-whom-h.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If angels are called sons, why are we adopted? Because the Word uses son for three different things. Angels are sons because Yahweh made them. Jesus is the Son because He was begotten, and He made the angels. We become sons by adoption, because the Son took on our nature, the nature made in His image, and never theirs (Hebrews 2:16). Here is how the Word keeps the three apart.
ll214-sons-of-yahweh-whom-he-made-whom-h.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Angels are sons too, so why are we adopted? Because there are three kinds of sonship and the Word never blends them. The angels were made, and they serve the heirs. The Son was begotten, and the angels worship Him. We are adopted, through the begotten Son who took the made nature of man, so that men and women could cry Abba, Father, and be heirs with Him. Not because we are greater than the angels, but because He took our nature and calls us brothers.

teen.open: Angels are called sons of Yahweh too. So why does the Bible say we are adopted? Because there are three kinds of sons: made, born, and adopted.
teen.close: So angels are sons because Yahweh made them. Jesus is the Son by birth. And you can be a son or daughter by adoption, because Jesus became a human like you.

senior.open: Scripture calls the angels sons, yet Hebrews says no angel was ever told, you are My Son. The answer lies in three words the Word keeps distinct: made, begotten, and adopted.
senior.close: So the title's question has a clear answer. The angels are sons by making, Jesus is the Son by begetting, and we are sons by adoption, because the Son took on human nature, not the nature of angels.

ll215-when-a-land-has-no-smith-count-the.reason: Long report summary and boundaries first; the three answers (count honestly, prepare small first, safety is of the LORD) are spread across sections one, three and four and only gathered in section ten.
ll215-when-a-land-has-no-smith-count-the.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does Yahweh's Word say to a nation that lost its smiths? Three things. Count the cost honestly before you build, and let honest arithmetic produce a smaller plan if it must (Luke 14:28-32). Prepare the work in the field first, where being wrong is cheap, and build the house after (Proverbs 24:27). And build the defences well, but do not trust them to save you: the horse is prepared, but safety is of the LORD (Proverbs 21:31).
ll215-when-a-land-has-no-smith-count-the.example: THE SUM THE PARABLE ASKS FOR. The report gives a stated need of two hulls a year against a delivered rate of about one and a third. That gap is the very sum Jesus tells a king to sit down and do first, publish truthfully, and act on. The new builder's choice to open a small facility years early and prove its methods on small parts before the great yard exists is the field before the house. Both moves are wise. Neither one is the safety.
ll215-when-a-land-has-no-smith-count-the.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your nation lost its smiths: what does the Word say? Repairing that lost capacity is honourable work, and doing it wisely means counting the cost truthfully, proving the small part before promising the great one, and holding other people's money as a faithful steward. But the safety was never in a hull, a yard, a balance sheet or a name on a door. Prepare the horse, and remember the name of the LORD. Safety is of Him, and that is where true safety comes from.

teen.open: When a country cannot build what it needs, what does the Word say? Count the cost honestly, start small and prove it, and remember real safety comes from Yahweh.
teen.close: So build carefully and do the math honestly. Then trust Yahweh, not the ships or the money, because safety is of the LORD.
