ll293-one-thing-is-needful.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If you were told plainly and still do it your way, what does obedience look like? It looks like doing exactly what was asked, because to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22), and a lot of hard work nobody asked for is not obedience. Patience, which the Word calls longsuffering, is long but not endless. And while you bear the load, you rest in Jesus, step apart, and share the weight. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll293-one-thing-is-needful.example: THE GIFT NOBODY ASKED FOR. Say a mother asks her son to clear the gutters before the rain. He spends Saturday building her a new garden bed instead, works hard, and expects thanks. The rain comes, the gutters overflow, and the basement floods. He worked more than he was asked, but he did not do what was asked. That is Saul's sacrifice in a small house. One plain sentence, written down and done first, would have kept the basement dry.
ll293-one-thing-is-needful.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Told plainly, still doing it your way? Yahweh wrote His will down plainly so you can run with it. Obedience is humbling yourself to exactly what was asked: the few words that carry the whole, done before the ninety-five that are all talk. When patience runs out, remember longsuffering is His fruit, long but not endless; live peaceably as much as lies in you, and where you are not bound, stop reproving the scorner. Where you must stay, bring the weight to Jesus and find rest for your soul (Matthew 11:28-29).

teen.open: If someone tells you exactly what they want, do that, not your own version. The Word says obeying matters more than doing something bigger nobody asked for.
teen.close: So do the one thing you were asked, first. Be patient with people, but you do not have to keep arguing with someone who will not listen. When it gets heavy, bring it to Jesus and rest.

senior.open: The title asks what obedience looks like when we have been told plainly. The Word answers: do exactly what was asked, bear others with a longsuffering that has limits, and rest in Him under the load.
senior.close: So the Word's answer is simple, if not easy. Obey what was written plainly, carry others with patience where the Word binds you, and take His yoke so your soul finds rest while you bear it.

ll294-a-prophet-in-his-own-house.reason: Opens on Darrell's question and Jesus rejected at home; how to love without losing the measure (say it once in love, live it, honor, separate in peace) is scattered and gathered only in the final practice.
ll294-a-prophet-in-his-own-house.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What do you do when family will not hear the one thing that matters? Jesus faced it first: His own brothers did not believe Him (John 7:5). The research shows why arguing harder fails: a belief tied to identity is defended like the self, and a flooded heart cannot hear. So you love without losing the measure: say the one thing once, in love, live it, keep honoring them, and let Yahweh do the changing. Here is how.
ll294-a-prophet-in-his-own-house.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. When family will not hear the one thing, you are walking the road Jesus walked, and His brothers were later found praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14). Do not feed the argument: name what you feel, and step away when your heart is pounding, as Lieberman and Gottman found. Say the one thing once, in love, then live it so they can be won without a word. Keep honoring and providing. If strife will not stop, separate in peace as Abram did, and keep watching the road. You keep the measure, and Yahweh does what an argument cannot.

teen.open: What if your family will not listen about what matters most? Jesus' own brothers did not believe Him at first. You can keep loving them without giving up what is true.
teen.close: So say it once, kindly, and then live it. Do not keep arguing. If your heart is racing, take a break. Pray for them, and let Yahweh do the changing.

senior.open: The title asks how to love family who will not hear the one thing that matters. Jesus faced this in His own house, and the Word and the research agree that arguing harder will not reach a defended heart.
senior.close: So keep the measure and keep the love. Speak the one thing once, plainly and gently, live it before them, honor and provide still, separate in peace if you must, and keep watching the road as the prodigal's father did.

ll296-willing-and-obedient.reason: Opens with a long list of Darrell's questions; the answers (Yahweh works the willing, set a watch on the mouth, five steps when evil is called good) are spread across sections; ends on talk prompts and a weekly list.
ll296-willing-and-obedient.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Do you really want to follow? On your own, no one makes themselves willing. Yahweh does: He draws you, writes His law on your heart, and gives you a new heart that wants to walk in His ways (Philippians 2:13; Ezekiel 36:26-27). He shapes the follower after His Son, who humbled Himself. He tames the tongue as you ask Him to set a watch before your mouth (Psalms 141:3). And when someone calls evil good, you pray, guard your own words, say the truth once, keep the record, and honor them anyway. Here is how the Word shows each part.
ll296-willing-and-obedient.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Do you really want to follow? If you do, it is because Yahweh worked that will in you; so the first move, for leader and follower alike, is prayer. He forms the follower after the Son, who chose to be under. He clothes that follower with humility, so they stop measuring a leader by their own untested standard. He sets a watch on the mouth, so the leader's plain words are said back, not slid. And when evil is called good, you pray, speak once, keep the record, honor them, and stay where the Word binds you. A willing heart is His gift, and it eats the good of the land (Isaiah 1:19).

teen.open: Do you really want to follow? Nobody makes themselves willing. Yahweh works that want in you, and He helps you watch your words too.
teen.close: So, do you want to follow? Ask Yahweh to make you willing. Say what your leader said back in their words before adding yours, and let Him guard your mouth.

senior.open: The title asks whether we truly want to follow. The Word answers that willingness is Yahweh's work in us (Philippians 2:13), and that He also teaches the humble heart, the guarded tongue, and a steady answer when evil is called good.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. A willing follower is made by Yahweh, shaped like the Son, clothed with humility, and kept by a watch on the mouth. When evil is called good, pray, speak once, keep the record, and honor them still.

ll298-what-programs-you.reason: Says early that the daily system programs you, but what it teaches (about people, time, worth, Yahweh) and how to check it only arrive near the end in the audit section; ends on a weekly to-do list.
ll298-what-programs-you.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Your daily system is teaching you something; what is it teaching? Whatever it was designed to teach. The plan, the feed, the way you keep score, the way you talk to yourself: each one trains you, by repetition, to see people, time, worth and Yahweh its way. The question is whether it teaches what Yahweh teaches. The thing you repeat that is not quality is the very thing He wants to rewrite. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll298-what-programs-you.example: ONE SYSTEM, LAID BESIDE THE WORD. Say your way of keeping score at work counts only what you finished today. Repeated every day, it quietly teaches that your worth is your output, and that a slow day makes you less. Lay that beside the Word: you are His temple, not your own (1 Corinthians 6:19), and His compassions are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22-23). Where they disagree, believe the Word. Keep the score, but change what it is allowed to tell you, and repeat the new way until it is the new pattern.
ll298-what-programs-you.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What is your daily system teaching you? Exactly what it was built to teach, every day, down to the root. So you do not stop using systems; you choose the one that programs you deepest. Name what you repeat, ask what it says about people, time, worth and Yahweh, and lay it beside the Word. Let a faithful friend show you the blind spot. Agree with the King's rewrite, and make His Word, read in the morning and meditated on day and night, the system underneath every other system. Then what your days teach you is what He teaches.

teen.open: What you do every day is teaching you something. Your phone, your schedule, how you talk to yourself: each one trains how you see life.
teen.close: So what is your daily system teaching you? Check it against the Word. Where they disagree, believe Yahweh, and repeat His way until it becomes your way.

senior.open: The title says your daily system is teaching you, and asks what. It teaches whatever it was designed to teach, and repetition writes it deep. The question is whether that matches what Yahweh teaches.
senior.close: So the answer is this: your daily system teaches you its own view of people, time and worth. Lay it beside the Word, agree with His rewrite, and let His Word become the system beneath all the others.

ll295-the-bleating-of-the-sheep.reason: Opens with Darrell's framing and Saul's story; the plain answer (knowing comes after doing the whole, John 7:17) and the leader's cost come in middle sections; ends on talk prompts and a weekly task.
ll295-the-bleating-of-the-sheep.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What is the difference between saying you follow and doing the whole thing, and why does it matter? Saying is not following (Luke 6:46). Understanding comes after doing the whole of what you were given (John 7:17), so the person who does only part never receives what only the whole can teach. The cost falls on the leader who bears it: grief, self-doubt when the truth is turned around, and a weariness the Word does not hide. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll295-the-bleating-of-the-sheep.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Saying you follow and doing the whole thing are not the same, and Saul's bleating sheep prove it. Part of a command called the whole blocks the understanding that only full obedience gives, which is why Naaman was healed only after dipping seven times, exactly as told. The leader who bears it carries grief, doubt and weariness, as Moses and Paul did. So take the weight to Yahweh first, write the steps plainly, check the work against the page without condemnation, keep the record, pour into those who truly follow, and keep the door open for the first works. Doing the whole is how you come to know.

teen.open: Saying you follow is not the same as doing all of it. If you only do part, you miss what doing the whole would have taught you.
teen.close: So what is the difference? Doing every step. Try following one instruction all the way this week, before adding your own ideas, and see what you learn.

senior.open: The title sets saying against doing. The Word is plain that calling Him Lord without doing what He says is not following (Luke 6:46), and that understanding is given to the one who does the whole (John 7:17).
senior.close: So the answer stands. Partial obedience keeps a person from the understanding the whole would give, and it weighs on the leader. Take that weight to Yahweh, check the work against the page, and keep the door open for the first works.

ll299-read-with-the-heart.reason: Answers early (count vs heart; Jesus asks how, not how often) and SAY IT AGAIN restates it, but the lesson then ends on family talk prompts and a general line, not on what Yahweh asks.
ll299-read-with-the-heart.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Thirty-eight reads and zero change? Then the count was never the measure. What Yahweh asks when you open the Word is how you hear, not how often (Luke 8:18). He asks for an honest and good heart that hears, understands, keeps and bears fruit with patience. Ask Him for open eyes, read slowly enough to say it back, come to the Son the Word testifies of, hide one line in your heart, and do one thing it asks today. A count looks on the outside. Yahweh looks on the heart, and one verse received there can change a life.

teen.open: You can read something many times and nothing changes. Yahweh cares less about how often you read and more about how you hear.
teen.close: So what does Yahweh ask when you open the Word? Read with your heart: ask Him to open your eyes, understand it, keep one line, and do what it says today.

senior.open: The title asks why many readings can leave us unchanged. Jesus' answer is to take heed how we hear (Luke 8:18): the measure is the manner of the heart, not the number of passes.
senior.close: So the answer is this. Yahweh asks for a heart that hears, understands, keeps and bears fruit with patience. Let the count be a record; let the heart be the measure, for He looks on the heart.

ll297-precept-upon-precept.reason: Opens with Darrell's thanksgiving; the plain answer (feelings are real but not a compass) sits mid-lesson in OFF THE EMOTIONAL SIDE; the daily-gap answer comes late; ends on a weekly to-do list.
ll297-precept-upon-precept.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Your feelings are loud, but are they a compass? No. Feelings are real and tell you something true about yourself, but they do not tell you what to do. Yahweh's Word does, one precept upon another. Read daily, it brings you off the emotional side so you decide steady instead of double-minded, it shows the gap you missed while it is still small, and it trains you, like an athlete, in the skill of following the King. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll297-precept-upon-precept.example: ONE DECISION, TWO MINDS. Say a hard message arrives and everything in you wants to answer it now, while the feeling is high. Your feelings pull one way and what you read this morning pulls another: two minds, the instability James names (James 1:5-8). So you stop. You reread the one precept you wrote down, ask Yahweh for wisdom, and wait until your mind is stayed on Him (Isaiah 26:3). The feeling still tells you something about you. The precept tells you what to do.
ll297-precept-upon-precept.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Are your feelings a compass? They are real, and they are honest about you, but they are not the compass. The compass is the Word, the counsel that hits the spot, a lamp that shows the next step. Taken daily like manna, precept upon precept, it brings you off the emotional side, makes you one-minded instead of double-minded, and lets it read you back. Daily is how the gaps stay small enough to see. That is the skill and discipline of following the King, and the King wants you to win.

teen.open: Strong feelings can feel like a map, but they are not. They tell you how you feel, not what to do. Yahweh's Word does that.
teen.close: So are your feelings a compass? No. Read a little of the Word every morning, and before a big choice made in strong feeling, reread it and ask Yahweh what He wants.

senior.open: The title asks whether loud feelings can guide us. The Word answers that feelings are real but are not a compass; the steady guide is Yahweh's counsel, given precept upon precept (Isaiah 28:9-10).
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Feelings report on us; the Word directs us. Gathered daily, it keeps us one-minded, catches small gaps before they widen, and trains us in the discipline of following the King.

ll300-put-not-your-trust-in-princes.reason: Opens on the election newsletter and promises the Word tells where to put the weight, but the answer (on Yahweh, Psalms 146:5; Jeremiah 17:7) only arrives in section SEVEN; THE LANDING then lands it well.
ll300-put-not-your-trust-in-princes.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. When the rulers let you down, where do you put your weight? On Yahweh, not on princes. Psalm 146 says not to trust in princes, because their breath goes forth and their plans perish, and calls the one whose hope is in the LORD happy (Psalms 146:3-5). Yahweh rules over the rulers. So you can still care, pray, vote and honor, while your full weight rests on Him. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll300-put-not-your-trust-in-princes.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. When the rulers let you down, where do you put your weight? On the One who removes and sets up kings, whose counsel stands for ever. Put not your trust in princes: their breath goes forth and their thoughts perish. So pray for whoever is in authority, honor the office without worshipping the man, vote and take counsel, and obey up to the line where a man asks what Yahweh forbids. Then lean your whole weight on Him. Like the tree by the river, the heat still comes, but your leaf stays green.

teen.open: When leaders disappoint you, where do you lean? Psalm 146 says not on rulers, but on Yahweh, who rules over every ruler.
teen.close: So where do you put your weight? On Yahweh. Pray for leaders, even ones you did not pick, and take part, but keep your hope in Him, not in them.

senior.open: The title asks where to put our weight when rulers disappoint. Psalm 146 answers plainly: not in princes, whose breath goes forth, but in the LORD, who reigns over every ruler.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. We pray for those in authority, honor the office, vote and take counsel, and obey up to the line of Acts 5:29. Our weight, though, rests on Yahweh, whose counsel stands for ever.

ll301-old-men-dream-young-men-see.reason: Opens on where Joel 2:28 is written and Pentecost; the direct answer (an old man's dream can reach past his lifetime, Hebrews 11:13; the promise is to your children, Acts 2:39) sits mid-lesson; ends on talk prompts.
ll301-old-men-dream-young-men-see.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can your dreams reach past your own lifetime? Yes, when they are from Yahweh. He promised to pour out His Spirit on all flesh, old and young, sons and daughters (Joel 2:28-29), and Peter said the promise is to you and to your children (Acts 2:39). Abraham died before he saw what he was promised, yet he saw it afar off (Hebrews 11:13). A dream from the Spirit, tested by the Word and told to the next generation, outlives the one who dreamed it. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll301-old-men-dream-young-men-see.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can your dreams reach past your own lifetime? The Word says yes. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost by the risen Jesus is for every generation, and the promise runs to your children, your children's children, and all that are afar off. Abraham and those like him died in faith, having seen the promise afar off. So weigh every dream against the Word, write the vision plainly, wait for His time, and tell it to the next generation. The old dream and tell, the young see and go, and what Yahweh gave you keeps speaking after you.

teen.open: Can a dream from Yahweh last longer than you do? Yes. His Spirit is for every age, young and old, and His promise goes to your children too.
teen.close: So can your dreams reach past your life? If they are from Yahweh, yes. Test them by the Word, write them down, and listen to the older people who dreamed before you.

senior.open: The title asks whether a dream can outlast the one who dreams it. Joel and Peter answer that the Spirit is poured on every generation, and Hebrews 11:13 shows faithful people who died seeing the promise afar off.
senior.close: So the answer is yes. A dream given by the Spirit, tested by the Word and written plainly, reaches past our years. Our part is to tell the next generation what Yahweh has done and promised.

ll302-a-standard-for-every-age.reason: After a long setup the first section answers (the standard lasts because its Author does not change); SAY IT AGAIN restates it, but the lesson ends on family talk prompts, not on the answer.
ll302-a-standard-for-every-age.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is there a moral rule that lasts forever? Yes. Treat others the way you want to be treated, the rule Jesus called the law and the prophets (Matthew 7:12), survives every age because its Author does not change (Malachi 3:6). Man's codes are rewritten; Yahweh's law is not. And the Author matters, because without Him the rule has no root, and none of us can keep it. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll302-a-standard-for-every-age.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is there a moral rule that lasts forever? There is, and the Golden Rule passes the test of every age because it is not man's rule but Yahweh's: written in stone, summed up by Jesus, and written on every conscience. Man's codes change; His law does not, because He changes not. That is why the Author matters. Remove Him and the rule becomes a cut flower, and the mind drifts toward the reprobate mind of Romans 1:28. Keep Him and the standard stands, and in Jesus, who died for us while we were yet sinners, it is finally kept.

teen.open: Is there a rule that never goes out of date? Yes. Treat others how you want to be treated. It lasts because Yahweh, who gave it, never changes.
teen.close: So does a moral rule last forever? Yes, because its Author does. People's rules change. Yahweh's does not, and Jesus helps us keep it.

senior.open: The title asks whether any moral rule can outlast every age. The Word answers yes: the Golden Rule is Jesus' summary of the law and the prophets (Matthew 7:12), and it lasts because Yahweh, its Author, does not change.
senior.close: So the answer stands. Human codes are amended and repealed; Yahweh's law is settled for ever. The rule fits every person because He wrote it on every heart, and it is kept only in Jesus.

ll303-what-good-is.reason: Builds a definition of good first; the plain answer (good that knows and does nothing is not good, James 4:17) arrives in the middle section THE SAYING CONTRADICTS ITSELF; ends on talk prompts.
ll303-what-good-is.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If good people stand still, is it still good? No. In Yahweh, being good and doing good are one: the psalmist says, "Thou art good, and doest good" (Psalms 119:68), and Jesus went about doing good. So good that knows what to do and does nothing is not yet the good the Word describes; to the one who knows to do good and does it not, it is sin (James 4:17). This is a mirror, not a whip. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll303-what-good-is.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. If good people stand still, is it still good? The Word answers no. Good is what Yahweh is and what He does, and in whoever He makes good, being and doing are one. The priest and the Levite were called good and passed by; the Samaritan showed mercy. The servant who hid his talent did nothing and was called wicked. We cannot produce this good in our flesh, but we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works. So do the good you know, today, and do not grow weary: in due season you will reap.

teen.open: Can someone be good while doing nothing when they see a need? The Word says real good moves. Yahweh is good, and He does good.
teen.close: So if good people stand still, is it still good? No. Good acts. Ask Yahweh for help, then do one good thing you know you should do today.

senior.open: The title asks whether goodness that stands still is still goodness. The Word answers that in Yahweh, being good and doing good are one (Psalms 119:68), so known good left undone is called sin (James 4:17).
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Goodness, as the Word defines it, acts. It grows as the Spirit's fruit in those joined to Christ, and it shows in mercy done. Do the good you know, and do not grow weary.

ll304-what-righteousness-is.reason: Opens on precept upon precept and Yahweh's nature; the answer to 'right in their own eyes' (no: Yahweh ponders the heart; none righteous; righteousness is a gift in Christ) arrives mid-lesson; ends on talk prompts.
ll304-what-righteousness-is.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Some say they are righteous. Is anyone right in their own eyes? Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but Yahweh ponders the heart (Proverbs 21:2), and He does not accept the verdict we pass on ourselves. None is righteous, no, not one (Romans 3:10). Righteousness is Yahweh's own nature, given to us as a gift in Christ, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS, and then lived out. Here are its seven jewels, line upon line.
ll304-what-righteousness-is.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is anyone right in their own eyes? Only in their own eyes. The Pharisee prayed with himself, called himself righteous, and went home unchanged; the publican asked for mercy and went home justified. Righteousness is Yahweh's nature and His standard, never our self-verdict. It is a gift, counted to Abraham and made ours in Jesus, the Lamb of Yahweh, worn as a robe. Then it is lived as a path, guards like a breastplate, and flows like a stream. And when you fall, confess: He is faithful and just to forgive.

teen.open: Can you decide for yourself that you are good enough? The Word says everyone looks right to themselves, but Yahweh looks at the heart.
teen.close: So is anyone right just because they think they are? No. Real righteousness is a gift from Jesus. Then you live it out, and when you mess up, you confess and He forgives.

senior.open: The title asks whether anyone can be righteous by their own judgment. Proverbs 21:2 answers that every way seems right to its owner, but Yahweh weighs the heart; true righteousness is His, and He gives it.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. No one is right by self-verdict. Righteousness is Yahweh's nature, given in Christ as a gift and robe, then lived as a path, a breastplate and a stream.

ll306-the-path-of-the-just-shineth.reason: Told as Darrell's testimony section by section; the how (work as to the Lord, give no occasion, no vengeance, promotion from Him) is scattered, and the shining (Proverbs 4:18) only lands late; ends on talk prompts.
ll306-the-path-of-the-just-shineth.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How does Yahweh keep you shining while you work someone else's project? You work as to the Lord, not to men (Colossians 3:23-24). You catch the little foxes, the small details, then settle and let Understanding come. He places a ram in the thicket, someone who helps, and uses people for you and against you to sharpen you. You give no occasion, take no vengeance, and run with patience, and promotion comes from Him. Here is how the Word and Darrell's working life show it.
ll306-the-path-of-the-just-shineth.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How does Yahweh keep you shining on someone else's project? By making Him your real Employer and keeping His Word first. Watch the little foxes, then relax and let Understanding come. Look for the ram in the thicket and the Jonathan He places beside you. Let friend and rival both sharpen you. Be faithful like Daniel, so no rule can be turned against you. Read fruit without prejudging, step aside from fights you can see coming, and hand every account to Him. Then the promise holds: the path of the just shines more and more unto the perfect day (Proverbs 4:18).

teen.open: Working for a hard boss or on someone else's plan? Yahweh can still make you shine, when you work for Him first and do not get even.
teen.close: So how do you keep shining? Do your work as if for Jesus, watch the small details, give no one a reason to blame you, and let Yahweh handle the people who are against you.

senior.open: The title asks how a person keeps shining while laboring on another's project, often under hard leadership. The Word answers: work as unto the Lord, give no occasion, take no vengeance, and let promotion come from Him.
senior.close: So the answer stands. Keep the Word first, attend to the small details, receive the helpers He sends, leave vengeance with Him, and run with patience. The path of the just shines more and more unto the perfect day.

ll305-search-me-and-know-my-heart.reason: Opens with the thread recap and Yahweh pondering the heart; the direct answer (a heart cannot audit itself; pray Psalm 139:23-24 and stay while He searches) sits in NOT ALONE; ends on talk prompts.
ll305-search-me-and-know-my-heart.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can your heart grade its own paper? No. The heart is deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9); left alone, it will grade itself and give itself an A. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but Yahweh ponders the heart (Proverbs 21:2). So you do consider and keep your heart, but you do it with Him, praying Psalm 139: search me, and know my heart. He brings the light; you hold still. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll305-search-me-and-know-my-heart.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can your heart grade its own paper? It cannot, and the Word never asks it to. Yahweh ponders the heart, so you ponder yours, considering your ways and keeping your heart with all diligence, but never alone. You pray, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalms 139:23), and stay while He searches. He wrote the code of your soul and knows it better than you do. Where He shows a gap, bring it to the Prince of Peace; where it is sin, ask for a clean heart. Then even the hard things you carry become bread for you.

teen.open: Can you check your own heart and trust the grade? Not really. Hearts go easy on themselves. That is why you look inside with Yahweh, not alone.
teen.close: So can your heart grade itself? No. Pray, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psalms 139:23). Let Him show you what needs fixing, and bring it to Jesus for peace.

senior.open: The title asks whether the heart can judge itself. The Word answers no: it is deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9), and only Yahweh, who ponders the heart, can search it truly.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. We are told to consider and keep our hearts, yet we do it in His presence, praying Psalm 139:23-24, and bringing every gap He shows us to the Prince of Peace.

ll307-love-walks-with-you-on-the-trainin.reason: The answer (Love walks with you while you learn, and keeps you honest in both directions) is one line in section two; the rest ranges widely (Godhead, brain, wealth, fatherless) and ends on talk prompts.
ll307-love-walks-with-you-on-the-trainin.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can you walk the training ground of good and evil with Love and still stay honest? Yes. Love does not wait at the finish line; according to Yahweh, Love walks with you while you learn. And Love keeps you honest in both directions: about the good and evil in yourself, where it is hardest to see, and in other people, where it is easiest to judge. Your discernment is trained by use (Hebrews 5:14), and He refines you in the fire without leaving. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll307-love-walks-with-you-on-the-trainin.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you walk the training ground with Love and still stay honest? The Word says yes, because the Love that walks with you suffers long and rejoices in the truth. It lets you admit the war inside, as Paul did, without despair, and it keeps you from judging others more harshly than yourself. Practice trains your senses; the fire refines, not abandons; and there is always a way to escape, so no evil is needed to make ends meet. The Father of the fatherless teaches what no one else taught. So walk it honestly, with Him beside you the whole way.

teen.open: Life is like a training ground where you learn what is good and what is evil. Yahweh's Love walks with you the whole time, and it keeps you honest.
teen.close: So can you learn good and evil with Love and stay honest? Yes. Be honest about your own mistakes, go easy on judging others, and keep practicing. Yahweh never leaves you.

senior.open: The title asks whether we can learn good and evil on life's training ground with Love and still remain honest. The lesson answers yes: Love walks with us while we learn, and keeps us truthful about ourselves and others.
senior.close: So the answer holds. The Love that suffers long also rejoices in the truth. Discernment is trained by use, the fire refines, and the way to escape is always provided, with Yahweh beside us throughout.

ll309-he-shall-stand-before-kings.reason: Diligence is anchored early, but 'not your final audience' (you serve the Lord Christ) appears only mid-lesson, and honest answers and peace come in separate later sections; ends on practice prompts.
ll309-he-shall-stand-before-kings.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why is your panel not your final audience, and how do you prepare for it? You walk into any interview room as a servant of Jesus: you serve the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:23-24). The panel is real and it matters, but He is the One you work for. So you prepare His way: diligent work done long before the invitation (Proverbs 22:29), honest answers on every form and in every room, and peace in place of fear (Philippians 4:6-7). Then you release the outcome to Him. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll309-he-shall-stand-before-kings.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Your panel is not your final audience, because the work was always done as to the Lord. That is why you prepare diligently: count the cost, know the posting, ready true stories, and test the room a day early. That is why you answer honestly, never rounding up, and take the seat that fits rather than the highest one. And that is why you can walk in with peace instead of fear. Pray before you answer, as Nehemiah did, give the credit to Yahweh, as Joseph did, and then let Him who gives promotion decide. Whatever the answer, you did the work for Him.

teen.open: Facing an interview or a big panel? They matter, but they are not your final audience. You are really working for Jesus.
teen.close: So who is your final audience? Jesus. Prepare well, tell the truth in every answer, pray before you speak, and trust Yahweh with how it turns out.

senior.open: The title says the panel is not our final audience. The Word explains why: whatever we do, we do as to the Lord (Colossians 3:23), and so diligence, honesty and peace become our preparation.
senior.close: So the answer is clear. We prepare diligently, answer truthfully, choose our seat soberly and enter with peace, because we serve the Lord Christ. Promotion comes from Him, and the outcome rests with Him.

ll310-the-hidden-life-and-the-empty-chai.reason: Opens with a long, careful news summary; the costs (soul first, family, a handle others can hold, a company with no successor) and Yahweh's way (Jethro, Joshua, 2 Timothy 2:2) are spread through later sections; ends on talk prompts.
ll310-the-hidden-life-and-the-empty-chai.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does a hidden life cost, and how does Yahweh prepare the next shepherd? What is covered will be uncovered (Luke 12:2). A hidden life costs the leader his own soul first (Proverbs 6:32), wounds a family and coworkers, and becomes a handle others can hold. A leader who carries everything alone, with no successor, wears away the people too (Exodus 18:18). Yahweh's way is faithful people sharing the load and a shepherd named and prepared before you go. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll310-the-hidden-life-and-the-empty-chai.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does a hidden life cost? First the soul, then the family and coworkers, and in time the public life it ends up governing, because what is covered comes to light. And the empty chair costs everyone who leaned on one person. Yahweh's answer to both is the same: walk in the light, run like Joseph rather than reach like David, and confess before you are found out. Then share the burden with able, faithful people, and lay hands on a Joshua before you go, so the people are not as sheep without a shepherd. That is a leader finished well.

teen.open: Secrets do not stay hidden forever, and leaders who do everything alone leave a hole when they fall. The Word shows a better way.
teen.close: So what does a hidden life cost? A lot, for you and the people around you. Bring secrets into the light, run from temptation like Joseph, and help train the people who come after you.

senior.open: The title asks what a hidden life costs and how Yahweh prepares a successor. The Word answers that what is covered will be revealed (Luke 12:2), and that Moses was told to share the load and lay hands on Joshua.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. A hidden life destroys the soul before it topples a company, and a leader with no successor leaves the people exposed. Confess and forsake, share the burden, and prepare the next shepherd.

ll311-every-man-presseth-into-it.reason: Opening paragraph already answers (keep your grip on Yahweh when you cannot see, and do not let go) and FAITH IS NOT PERFORMANCE lands it, but the lesson ends on talk prompts rather than the answer.
ll311-every-man-presseth-into-it.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What do Jacob, Elijah and the bleeding woman teach about holding on to Yahweh in the dark? That the force the kingdom honors is not a shout but a grip. Jacob, wounded, wept and would not let go until he was blessed. Elijah lay under a tree and told Yahweh the truth, and was fed. The woman came in the press, touched His garment, and told Him all the truth. Even John brought his doubt to Jesus and was honored. So bring your fear and your mixed faith to Him, and hold on. You hold because you are held, and no man can pluck you out of His hand.

teen.open: Faith is not about being the loudest. It is about holding on to Yahweh, even when things are dark and confusing.
teen.close: So how do you hold on in the dark? Like Jacob, Elijah and the woman did: go to Yahweh honestly, tell Him the truth, and do not let go. He is holding you too.

senior.open: The title contrasts a shout with a grip. Read in its own place, Matthew 11:12 describes not swagger but people who press into the kingdom and keep their hold on Yahweh when they cannot see.
senior.close: So the answer stands. Holding on to Yahweh in the dark looks like Jacob's tears, Elijah's honesty and the woman's reach. Bring even doubt to Him; we hold because we are held, and none can pluck us from His hand.

ll308-only-yahweh-can-judge-me.reason: The first section answers (study what He will judge: fear Him, keep His commandments, 2 Timothy 2:15), but the lesson ranges wide (boasting, enemies, politics, money) and ends on talk prompts, not the answer.
ll308-only-yahweh-can-judge-me.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If only Yahweh judges you, what should you study? Study what He will judge you for. Solomon's conclusion is to fear Him and keep His commandments, because He brings every work into judgment, every secret thing (Ecclesiastes 12:13-14). So the saying is not a shield against correction; it is a summons to study and show yourself approved (2 Timothy 2:15). That study reaches your boasting, your enemies, your money and your hope. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll308-only-yahweh-can-judge-me.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. If only Yahweh judges you, what should you study? Whatever He judges, and the lesson walked it: boast only that you know Him; love the people you call enemies, because your fight is not with flesh and blood; do the good you already agree on; know who Jesus really is; study to own as His steward, spreading a portion to seven and also to eight. Above it all stands the winning hand, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus, bought with His precious blood. Study that, be at peace with Him through Jesus, and life becomes beautiful, hard and beautiful at once.

teen.open: You may have heard that only Yahweh can judge you. If that is true, the smart move is to learn what Yahweh cares about and will judge.
teen.close: So what should you study? What Yahweh will judge: how you boast, how you treat people who hurt you, how you handle money. Learn His Word, and walk in what Jesus won for you.

senior.open: The title takes a familiar saying seriously. If Yahweh alone is Judge, the wise response is to study what He will judge, for He brings every work into judgment (Ecclesiastes 12:14).
senior.close: So the answer is plain. We study what He judges: where we boast, how we treat those against us, how we steward what is His. And we rest in the winning hand, the life given us in Christ Jesus.

ll313-children-are-a-heritage-when-the-s.reason: Opens with a long reported news summary and a section on heritage; the answer (the house is the first schoolhouse, Deuteronomy 6:7) arrives only in the third section; ends on talk prompts.
ll313-children-are-a-heritage-when-the-s.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Schools are closing, but who is still teaching your children? The house is. Yahweh gave the charge to teach children to the home first: when you sit in your house, walk by the way, lie down and rise up (Deuteronomy 6:7). Not one of those places is a classroom. So whatever school a family uses, or loses, the first school never closes, and the church can help the children who fall behind. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll313-children-are-a-heritage-when-the-s.example: ONE DAY, FOUR CLASSROOMS. Say a family's neighborhood school closes and the bus ride gets longer. At breakfast, a parent reads one verse aloud: rising up. On the longer drive, they talk about what it means: walking by the way. After school, a grandmother at the kitchen table helps with reading: sitting in the house. At bedtime, the child says the verse back: lying down. No building is needed for any of it. The school changed; the first classroom did not.
ll313-children-are-a-heritage-when-the-s.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Schools are closing, so who is still teaching your children? You are, and the Word always meant it that way. Children are a heritage of the LORD, not a line item. The first schoolhouse is the house, at the table, on the way, at bedtime and first thing. Count the whole cost before you change a child's world, and let the church welcome the children who are riding farther and reading less. Jesus took the children in His arms, and the promise still stands: all thy children shall be taught of the LORD (Isaiah 54:13).

teen.open: Some schools are closing, but your learning does not stop. Yahweh says the first place you are taught is home.
teen.close: So who is still teaching you? Your family, at the table, in the car, at bedtime. Ask a parent or grandparent what they know of Yahweh, and learn it together.

senior.open: The title asks who teaches the children when schools close. The Word answers that the charge was given to the house first (Deuteronomy 6:6-7), and it does not close with any building.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. Children are a heritage, the home is the first classroom, and grandparents and churches are teachers too. Whatever school a family uses, the Word is still taught at the table and by the way.

ll314-will-my-work-live-on.reason: Opens on the essay and Solomon's twenty years of building; the plain answer (work built on Jesus Christ abides, children taught) only arrives in THE FIRST ANSWER near the end; closes on a family-talk prompt.
ll314-will-my-work-live-on.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Will your work outlast you? A building, a collection or a name in stone will not carry you forward; people forget, and even Solomon's houses could not hand down wisdom to his son. What lasts is work built on the one foundation, Jesus Christ, children taught the Word day by day, and a life spent fearing Yahweh and keeping His commandments. He keeps the record. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll314-will-my-work-live-on.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Will your work outlast you? Not because of its size or the name carved on it. Solomon built for twenty years and called it vanity, and the son who came after him forsook wise counsel. Joseph wanted his bones carried home, not a place among Egypt's treasures. Work outlasts you when it stands on Jesus Christ and survives the fire (1 Corinthians 3:11-14), when your children are taught and walk in truth, and when you have done your duty before Him. Yahweh keeps a book of remembrance. What He establishes is for ever.

teen.open: Will what you build last after you are gone? Not because your name is on it. It lasts when it is built on Jesus and passed on to people who know Him.
teen.close: So, will your work outlast you? Buildings and names get forgotten. Work built on Jesus, and the truth you pass on to others, is what Yahweh keeps for ever.

senior.open: The title asks whether your work will outlast you. Scripture answers plainly: monuments and names fade, but work built on Jesus Christ, and children taught to walk in truth, abide.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. Your work outlasts you when it rests on the one foundation, Jesus Christ, and is handed to faithful people. Yahweh keeps His own book of remembrance, and what He establishes stands for ever.

ll316-riches-make-themselves-wings.reason: Long opening on the newsletter's figures; which riches stay (treasure in heaven, good works, what the Blood bought) is spread across the steward and Blood sections and never stated as one answer; ends on a family prompt.
ll316-riches-make-themselves-wings.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If $2.5 trillion can fly away in one day, what riches stay? Market value is only a price resting on what people believe about tomorrow, so it can vanish without a factory falling. The riches that stay are the ones no market can mark down: trust in the living Yahweh, a life rich in good works, treasure laid up in heaven, and the redemption Jesus bought with His own Blood. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll316-riches-make-themselves-wings.example: ONE NUMBER, TWO KINDS OF RICHES. Say a family's retirement statement read $300,000 on Wednesday and $280,000 on Friday. Nothing in the house changed; the price people would pay changed. That is the eagle with wings. Now say that same family had set aside a cash cushion, paid down a debt, and given steadily to a neighbor in need. None of that moved on Friday. The first is a price that can change by morning; the second is what was actually done with what they had.
ll316-riches-make-themselves-wings.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What riches stay when trillions fly away in a day? Not market value, which was a shared expectation all along, and not barns we tell our souls to rest on. Riches stay when you know what you truly have, refuse to trust it, put it to work for others, and stay content up or down (1 Timothy 6:17-19). Treasure laid up in heaven cannot be stolen or rusted, and what the Lamb purchased with His Blood has no wings. That is the one treasure no market can mark down.

teen.open: Billions of dollars disappeared in one day. So what kind of riches actually stay? The Word says: trusting Yahweh, doing good for others, and what Jesus bought for you.
teen.close: So what stays? Not prices on a screen. What stays is treasure in heaven, good done for others, and the salvation Jesus bought with His Blood. No market can take that.

senior.open: When market value can vanish in an afternoon, the title asks which riches remain. The Word's answer is plain: riches built on trust in Yahweh, good works, and the redemption of Christ do not fly.
senior.close: So the question has its answer. Uncertain riches make themselves wings, but trust in the living Yahweh, a life rich in good works, and the redemption bought with the precious Blood of Christ remain, whatever the market does tomorrow.

ll315-of-one-blood.reason: The plain No (the Blood of Jesus, not lineage, makes clean; nothing in a family line hinders baptism) sits mid-lesson in THE ONE BLOOD THAT MATTERS; ends on Micah 6:8 after a long history section.
ll315-of-one-blood.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Could a church law overrule your baptism? No. In 1449 a law in Toledo acted as if a convert's family line outweighed his baptism, but the Word says Yahweh made all nations of one blood, that all baptized into Christ are one in Him, and that only the Blood of Jesus makes anyone clean. No law of men can rebuild a wall Jesus broke down. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll315-of-one-blood.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Could a church law overrule your baptism? Not before Yahweh. The purity-of-blood statutes ranked baptized people by lineage, and that ladder spread for centuries, but the Word answered it first: one blood for all nations (Acts 17:26), one body in Christ (Galatians 3:26-28), no stain handed down from father to son (Ezekiel 18:20). When the Ethiopian asked what hindered his baptism, nothing in his family line did. The Blood of the Lamb gathers people out of every kindred and cleanses from all sin. No council and no crown can undo what His Blood has done.

teen.open: Could a rule made by church leaders cancel your baptism because of your family line? No. The Bible says everyone comes from one blood, and only Jesus' Blood makes us clean.
teen.close: So, could a church law overrule your baptism? No. Your family line does not decide your worth. In Jesus you are one with every believer, and His Blood is what makes you clean.

senior.open: The title asks whether a church law could overrule a person's baptism, as the Toledo statute of 1449 tried to do by lineage. The Word answers no: all nations are of one blood, and Christ's Blood alone cleanses.
senior.close: So the answer stands. No statute of men can rank baptized believers by their ancestry. Yahweh is no respecter of persons, Christ has broken down the middle wall, and His Blood redeems out of every kindred and nation.

ll317-who-judges-greatness.reason: Long preamble on the essay before the answer (Yahweh judges, not critic or crowd; the greatest serves) emerges across middle sections; the SAY IT AGAIN summary lands it but the lesson ends on a talk prompt.
ll317-who-judges-greatness.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who really decides what is great? Not the crowd, and not the critics either; both are courts made of men, and the same crowd that cried Hosanna cried Crucify within a week. Yahweh decides, because He alone looks on the heart, and His measure is plain: the greatest is the one who serves. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll317-who-judges-greatness.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who really decides what is great? The crowd can be steered in a week, and the critic can be wrong too; what is highly esteemed among men can be abomination in Yahweh's sight (Luke 16:15). The stone the builders refused became the head of the corner, and the Father's verdict on His Son stood after the cross. So greatness is not a count of who is watching. It is whom you served, how faithfully, and for whose glory, measured by fruit. Yahweh judges, and His verdict is the only one that lasts.

teen.open: Who decides what is great: the crowd, the critics, or someone else? The same crowd that cheered Jesus later yelled for His death. Yahweh decides, and He says the greatest is the one who serves.
teen.close: So who decides what is great? Not likes, views or the crowd. Yahweh sees your heart, and in His eyes the greatest person is the one who serves others.

senior.open: The title asks who truly decides what is great. The Word answers that neither the critic nor the crowd holds that seat; Yahweh judges by the heart, and Jesus defined greatness as service.
senior.close: So the question is answered. Men's esteem, whether of experts or of multitudes, is not Yahweh's verdict. He looks on the heart, He exalted the Son the crowd rejected, and He counts as greatest the one who serves.

ll319-what-the-trust-could-not-keep.reason: Spends its first third on the trust filings and GRAT mechanics; the answer (a trust protects shares, not the heart, marriage or name; guard your heart) arrives mid-lesson; ends on a talk prompt.
ll319-what-the-trust-could-not-keep.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What can a decade-old trust not protect, and what does the Word ask you to guard? A trust can move shares safely to heirs, and planning for your grandchildren is wise. But no document can hold a man's heart, his marriage, his good name or a father's example. The Word tells you to guard your heart with all diligence, because out of it are the issues of life (Proverbs 4:23). Plan your money; plan your heart harder.
ll319-what-the-trust-could-not-keep.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What could the trust not protect? The shares were out of reach of the storm; the man, the marriage and the name were not. A trust passes shares; it cannot pass a clean conscience, a faithful marriage or a father's example. So the Word asks you to guard your heart, keep the marriage bed undefiled, choose a good name over riches, and teach your children diligently. If you have fallen, David's road is open: confess, forsake, and receive mercy new every morning. The inheritance that lasts is a just man walking in his integrity, and his children blessed after him.

teen.open: A rich man planned his money perfectly for ten years, but not his heart. What can a plan for money never protect? Your heart, your name and the people you love. Those you have to guard yourself.
teen.close: So what can a money plan not protect? Your heart and your good name. Guard your heart every day, because everything in your life flows out of it.

senior.open: The title asks what a carefully built trust cannot protect. The Word's answer is the heart: a document can carry wealth to heirs, but not integrity, a faithful marriage or a good name. Those must be guarded.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Plan the estate wisely, for that is commended, but guard the heart with greater diligence. A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and the just man's children are blessed after him.

ll320-go-to-the-ant-keep-your-own-work-w.reason: Why Yahweh sends you back to your own field (no gladness at a fall; prove your own work; prepare in summer) is spread across middle sections; ends on the Lamb after a talk prompt, without gathering the answer.
ll320-go-to-the-ant-keep-your-own-work-w.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. When the market cheers a rival's fall, why does Yahweh send you back to your own field? Because gladness at another's fall displeases Him (Proverbs 24:17-18), and because your measure is your own work, not someone else's failure (Galatians 6:4-5). Like the ant, you are to work faithfully with no one watching, and to prepare in summer, long before anyone stumbles. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll320-go-to-the-ant-keep-your-own-work-w.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does Yahweh send you back to your own field when a rival falls? Because another's fall is not your harvest. He forbids the glad heart at a stumble, and He tells every person to prove his own work and bear his own burden. The rival in this story was ready because the work was done before the headline. So consider the ant: work with no overseer, gather in summer, know the state of your flocks, and trust Yahweh rather than any arm of flesh. Tend your field, weep with those who weep, and go to the Lamb when you fail.

teen.open: When someone you compete with messes up, why does Yahweh tell you to focus on your own work? Because being glad when others fall displeases Him, and your work is what you answer for.
teen.close: So why go back to your own field? Because someone else's failure is not your win. Like the ant, keep working faithfully even when nobody is watching, and do not cheer when others fall.

senior.open: The title asks why, when the world cheers a rival's fall, Yahweh sends us back to our own work. The Word answers that rejoicing at a fall displeases Him, and each person is measured by his own faithful labor.
senior.close: So the answer stands. Another's fall is not ours to celebrate or to build upon. Yahweh asks each of us to prove our own work, prepare in season as the ant does, and trust Him rather than men.

ll318-let-peter-answer-the-rock-the-keys.reason: Builds the answer step by step (revealed confession, Peter's own words in Acts 4 and 1 Peter 2, Christ the one foundation) but never states it plainly up front; ends on a talk prompt and Proverbs 27:17.
ll318-let-peter-answer-the-rock-the-keys.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who is the rock Jesus meant? Let Peter answer. When he preached and when he wrote, Peter called Jesus the stone the builders refused, the chief corner stone, and called himself a fellow elder and the believers lively stones laid on Him. The confession that Jesus is the Christ was revealed by the Father, and the One confessed is the foundation. Here is how the Word explains the Word.
ll318-let-peter-answer-the-rock-the-keys.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who is the rock Jesus meant? Peter himself tells you. He confessed by the Father's revelation that Jesus is the Christ, and eight verses later he was rebuked for speaking from his own wisdom. Years later he pointed to Jesus as the stone set at nought and made the head of the corner (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:6-7), and Paul agrees: other foundation can no man lay than Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). Peter used real keys to open doors by preaching, but the keys of death belong to Jesus. The church stands on Him, and so the gates cannot hold it.

teen.open: When Jesus talked about building His church on a rock, who did He mean? Let Peter answer. Peter himself called Jesus the corner stone, and called believers living stones built on Him.
teen.close: So who is the rock? Peter never called himself the foundation. He pointed to Jesus, the corner stone. The church is built on Jesus, and that is why nothing can hold it down.

senior.open: The title asks whom Jesus meant by the rock in Matthew 16. The surest answer is Peter's own: in Acts 4 and 1 Peter 2 he names Jesus the chief corner stone and counts himself a fellow elder.
senior.close: So the question is answered from Peter's own pen. The confession was revealed by the Father, the foundation is Jesus Christ, and Peter is one of the living stones built upon Him, a forgiven servant who opened doors by preaching.

ll321-lay-hands-suddenly-on-no-man.reason: Opens on the reported petition; the No (fitness is proved, not petitioned; those charged decide by witnesses) builds through the middle and is summed in SAY IT AGAIN, then the lesson ends on a talk prompt.
ll321-lay-hands-suddenly-on-no-man.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Should a petition decide who leads? No. The Word separates two things: forgiveness, which is given freely and quickly to anyone who confesses, and fitness to lead, which is proved over time, not petitioned. A petition is a headcount. The decision belongs to those charged with oversight, weighing witnesses and counsel without favour, and promotion itself belongs to Yahweh. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll321-lay-hands-suddenly-on-no-man.example: THREE QUESTIONS AT A SMALLER TABLE. Say a church member is asked to sign a note asking that a coach who stepped down last week be put back with the youth team right away. Before signing, the lesson's three questions apply. Has it been proved, or only regretted? Have the people charged with deciding had time to hear both sides? Am I backing him for who he is, or for what he brings the team? The coach can be forgiven today. The trust is restored on proof.
ll321-lay-hands-suddenly-on-no-man.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Should a petition decide who leads? The Word says no. Saul lost a kingdom because he obeyed the people's voice, and Pilate pleased the crowd on the worst day in history. Forgive fast and restore the person gently (Galatians 6:1). Restore the office slowly, on proof, as Jesus restored Peter with a question about love, not a crowd. Let those charged decide, by two or three witnesses and without partiality. Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither in the rush out nor in the rush back (1 Timothy 5:22). The crowd is not the judge.

teen.open: Should a big petition with thousands of names decide who gets to lead? No. You can forgive someone right away, but trusting them to lead again has to be earned and proved.
teen.close: So should a petition decide who leads? No. Forgive quickly, but let the right people decide about leading, slowly and fairly, after they have heard both sides. A crowd is not a judge.

senior.open: The title asks whether a petition of many names should decide who leads. Scripture says no: forgiveness is freely given, but fitness for an office is proved, and the decision rests with those charged with oversight.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. Forgive readily and restore the person in meekness, but restore the office only on proof, by due process and without partiality. A multitude of counsellors brings safety; a multitude of signatures does not.

ll323-count-the-cost-before-you-build-st.reason: Teaches the how-to in many scattered sections (sit down first, Nehemiah's survey, counsel, order, prove, tell truly) but never gathers it into one answer; ends on a talk prompt rather than the steps.
ll323-count-the-cost-before-you-build-st.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Before you press submit, how do you count the cost of a new tool and tell your own story truly? Sit down first and ask what it solves, what it costs to finish, and what happens to people if it fails. Survey the real state of things, bring the people who will carry it to the table, put order around it, and prove every result. Then speak of your own work soberly and truly, without rounding up. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll323-count-the-cost-before-you-build-st.example: TWO WAYS TO SAY IT. Say a letter needs to describe a project where you worked with five colleagues to set up a new scheduling tool. One way says, I transformed the whole organization. The other says, I coordinated a team of five that brought in a new scheduling tool, and we reviewed it with the staff who used it. The second is true, names the people, and lets the results speak. Anyone who checks will find the same.
ll323-count-the-cost-before-you-build-st.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How do you count the cost before you press submit? Do what the lesson walked through: sit down and count like the tower builder (Luke 14:28), view the wall like Nehemiah before announcing anything, let the people who carry the tool strengthen their own hands, share the load as Moses did, prove all things, and keep learning by use. Tell your own story soberly and truly, naming the team. Review everything before you send, then commit the work to Yahweh and rest, content whether the door opens or closes. That is how your gift makes room for you, by serving others truly (Proverbs 18:16).

teen.open: Before you hit submit on something new, how do you get it right? Stop and count the cost, ask the people it affects, test it, and when you talk about yourself, tell the truth plainly.
teen.close: So how do you count the cost? Plan first, check everything, include other people, and be honest about what you did. Then trust Yahweh with the result, whatever happens.

senior.open: The title asks how to count the cost of a new tool and present your own work truly. The Word's pattern is to sit down first, survey honestly, seek counsel, set order, prove the results, and speak of yourself soberly.
senior.close: So the answer is a settled order: count the cost, prepare the field, involve the people, test what the tool produces, and tell your story without exaggeration. Then commit the work to the LORD and be content with where He directs.

ll322-why-should-he-take-away-thy-bed.reason: Opens on the lender's email; the answer (the Word asks what a pledge could take because Yahweh fenced the bed, mill and house off from lenders; lower payment is not lower cost) sits mid-lesson; ends on a talk prompt.
ll322-why-should-he-take-away-thy-bed.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. When an offer promises a lower payment, why does the Word ask what it could take away? Because a lower payment is not a lower cost, and rolling cards into a loan against your home moves those debts onto your house. Yahweh's law kept lenders away from the bed a family sleeps in, the mill it eats from and the house it lives behind. So the Word asks, if you cannot pay, why should he take away your bed (Proverbs 22:27)?
ll322-why-should-he-take-away-thy-bed.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does the Word ask what a lower payment could take away? Because the headline speaks of relief and the small print speaks of the house. Yahweh would not let a lender keep a poor man's coat overnight, take the millstone, or walk into a home to choose a pledge. A card balance never touched the bed; a loan against the home puts it inside the fence by your own signature, and may cost more in total besides. So read the small print first, count the whole tower, seek counsel, and pay debts down one at a time instead of moving them. Sell, pay, live, and keep the bed.

teen.open: An offer says your monthly payment will be lower. Why does the Bible ask what you could lose? Because a smaller payment can cost more overall, and putting debts on your home could cost you the home.
teen.close: So why ask what it could take? Because a lower payment is not a lower cost. Read the small print, get advice, and pay debts off instead of risking the place your family lives.

senior.open: The title asks why Scripture questions what a lower-payment offer could take away. Because securing ordinary debts against a home moves them inside the fence Yahweh's law drew around a family's bed, mill and house.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. A lighter month can mean a heavier whole, and a pledged house can be lost. Read the disclosure before the headline, take counsel, and pay what is owed without placing the home beneath it.

ll325-god-is-able.reason: Rich in Yahweh's ability, but the title's practical question (what you do with almost nothing) is only implied in the widow story: start with what you have, seek counsel, obey; ends on the anchor verse and talk prompts.
ll325-god-is-able.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What do you do when you have almost nothing? You start with what is in the house, however small, as the widow did with one pot of oil. You go for counsel instead of sitting alone with the need, you obey what you are told, and you trust that Yahweh is able to make all grace abound toward you (2 Corinthians 9:8). He proves it in four places: lack, a turned road, weakness, and the furnace.
ll325-god-is-able.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What do you do when you have almost nothing? Do what the widow did: name what you have, ask for counsel, and obey; the oil kept flowing while there were vessels to fill, and the debt was paid. When the road is turned against you, remember Joseph, whose hard road saved many. When the thorn stays, hear that His grace is sufficient. When the furnace is hot, stand like the three young men, knowing He is able; the king saw a fourth walking with them in the fire. Almost nothing in your hands is never almost nothing in His. Yahweh is able.

teen.open: What do you do when you have almost nothing? Start with the little you have, ask for good advice, and obey Yahweh. He is able to do far more with it than you can picture.
teen.close: So what do you do with almost nothing? Give Yahweh what you have and trust Him. He filled the widow's jars, turned Joseph's hard road to good, and walked in the fire with His people. He is able.

senior.open: The title asks what to do when you have almost nothing. Like the widow of 2 Kings 4, begin with what is in the house, seek counsel, and obey, trusting that Yahweh is able to supply all sufficiency.
senior.close: So the answer is clear. Offer what little you have, take counsel, and walk in obedience. In lack, in redirection, in weakness and in the fire, the Word shows Yahweh able, and His grace is sufficient.

ll324-filled-to-devise-cunning-works.reason: Opens on the grant call; the yes (Yahweh filled makers like Bezaleel first, and the gift is to serve, be taught on and point to Jesus) comes in section two and spreads out; ends on a talk prompt.
ll324-filled-to-devise-cunning-works.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Could your craft be a calling? Yes. The first people the Word says Yahweh filled with His spirit for a task were makers: tailors, and Bezaleel, filled with wisdom, understanding and knowledge to devise cunning works. Craft becomes a calling when it serves the people, follows a plan written plainly, is handled honestly, is taught to others, seeks the peace of the city, and points past itself to Jesus. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll324-filled-to-devise-cunning-works.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Could your craft be a calling? The Word says it can. Yahweh called Bezaleel by name and filled him to make the place where He met His people. That calling worked from a written pattern, counted the cost, kept honest hands on the money, joined many crafts together, and put it in his heart to teach. It sought the good of the people and gave the blessing back to the One who filled him. So make good work for your community, plan it on one page, pass it on, and let it point to Jesus, the true tabernacle. Then your craft is not decoration; it is a calling.

teen.open: Could the thing you love to make be a calling from Yahweh? Yes. The first people the Bible says He filled with His spirit for a job were makers, like Bezaleel.
teen.close: So can your craft be a calling? Yes. When you use your skill to serve people, plan it well, teach others, and point to Jesus, your making is part of what Yahweh gave you to do.

senior.open: The title asks whether a craft can be a calling. The Word answers yes: Yahweh filled Bezaleel with wisdom, understanding and knowledge for all manner of workmanship, and gave him a heart to teach.
senior.close: So the question has its answer. A craft is a calling when it is received as Yahweh's gift, planned plainly, stewarded honestly, passed to others, and offered for the peace of the city and the glory of Christ.

ll326-touch-not-mine-anointed.reason: Answers each sub-question in turn, but the title's two answers (yes, now, by repentance and asking; He puts His Spirit within and seals openly) sit in the fourth and fifth sections; ends on a talk prompt.
ll326-touch-not-mine-anointed.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can you really receive the Spirit today, and how does He join Himself to you? Yes. The promise is to you and your children and all whom the Lord calls: repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, and receive the gift of the Holy Ghost (Acts 2:38-39). The adversary works by subtlety, but Yahweh comes in by the front door. He gives a new heart, puts His own Spirit within, and seals you openly.
ll326-touch-not-mine-anointed.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you receive the Spirit today, and how does He join Himself to you? Yes. Paul and John wrote in the present tense to ordinary believers: He has anointed us, sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts. The door is repentance and baptism in Jesus' name, asking, and obeying; the Spirit cannot be bought. He does not sneak in as the serpent did. He gives a new heart, dwells in you, makes your body His temple, and shows Himself in fruit: love, joy, peace. And greater is He that is in you than he that is in the world (1 John 4:4).

teen.open: Can you really receive Yahweh's Spirit today? Yes. When you turn to Jesus, are baptized, and ask, He puts His Spirit inside you, openly, not in secret.
teen.close: So can you receive the Spirit now? Yes. He gives you a new heart, lives in you, and grows good fruit like love and peace. And He is greater than anything in the world.

senior.open: The title asks whether the Spirit is received today and how He joins Himself to a life. The Word answers yes: through repentance, baptism and asking, Yahweh puts His Spirit within and seals His people.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. The anointing is not only for priests and kings of old; every believer sealed in Christ receives it. Yahweh gives a new heart, dwells within, and is known by the fruit He grows.

ll327-let-there-be-search-made.reason: The comment-period section says early that anyone may comment before a rule binds, and Ezra 5-6 shows the ruler hearing and searching first; but the lesson ends on household-papers talk prompts, not the answer.
ll327-let-there-be-search-made.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Before a rule binds you, who gets to be heard? Anyone with something true to say, in the lawful window, and a just ruler hears before he rules. In Ezra the governor asked his question, wrote down the elders' answer fairly, and asked the king to search the record before deciding. Here is how the Word shows the pattern, and how to speak into it well.
ll327-let-there-be-search-made.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Before a rule binds you, who gets to be heard? Everyone the rule touches may speak in the lawful window, and the Word expects the one who rules to hear before he answers (Proverbs 18:13). Ezra shows the whole pattern: a fair account, one plain ask, a search of the record, and a decision made after the roll was found, while the builders kept building. So pray first, honour the office, speak once with grace and facts, then go back to work. And keep your own papers findable, because a right on paper is only as useful as the paper is found. The outcome rests in Yahweh's hand.

teen.open: Before a new rule affects you, who gets to speak up? Anyone it touches can, honestly and respectfully. And good leaders listen and check the facts before they decide.
teen.close: So who gets heard? You do, if you speak at the right time, kindly and truthfully. Then keep doing your work, keep your records where you can find them, and trust Yahweh with the result.

senior.open: The title asks who is heard before a rule takes hold. Ezra 5 and 6 answer that those affected may speak, and that a just ruler searches the record and hears both sides before he decides.
senior.close: So the answer stands. A lawful, gracious word offered in its season deserves a hearing, and the honour of kings is to search out a matter. Speak plainly, keep your own records findable, and leave the outcome to Yahweh.

ll328-faithful-in-that-which-is-least-tr.reason: States the answer in its opening (trust is earned again; Luke 16:10) and builds it well, but the closing section is talk prompts about promises and schools, so the reader does not finish on the answer.
ll328-faithful-in-that-which-is-least-tr.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why is trust not a receipt? Because the Word treats it as a record that keeps being written. The master gave a few things first and said well done only after faithfulness was proved. Stewards must be found faithful, which means discovered by the people who look, and they must deal honestly in the sight of men as well as the Lord. A finished checklist is not yet fruit; the measure is the child who now reads. So whether you hold a vote, a vow or a job, write the next line faithfully today. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10).

teen.open: Is trust something you earn once and keep forever? No. Yahweh's Word shows that trust is built again every day by keeping small promises.
teen.close: So trust is not a receipt you file away. It is a record you keep writing, one faithful choice at a time. Be faithful in small things, and you will be trusted with more.

senior.open: The title says trust is not a receipt. The Word agrees: faithfulness is proved first and found by others, and it is earned again through daily decisions, not secured by a single vote or vow.
senior.close: So the point is settled. Trust is a record written each ordinary day, and fruit, not a finished list, is its proof. He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.

ll329-what-mean-these-stones.reason: Names the drift early but the why (eyes adjust, most on full days; forgetting is a silence nobody broke) and the remedy (set up stones) are spread over middle sections; ends on talk prompts after the Lord's table.
ll329-what-mean-these-stones.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why do yesterday's miracles start to feel like furniture? Because the wonder does not shrink; our eyes adjust. The Word warns that forgetting starts on the full days, not the hard ones, and Israel stood over daily manna and said there was nothing there. Yahweh's remedy is memorials that make a child stop and ask, and a choice to remember out loud. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll329-what-mean-these-stones.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why do yesterday's miracles feel like furniture? Because people adapt, and when we have eaten and are full, we stop seeing who gave the table. The manna lay on the ground every morning, and still they said there was nothing. Forgetting is rarely a decision; it is a silence nobody broke, and a generation rose that knew not the LORD. So set up stones: a written list of what Yahweh has done, told at the table, read aloud on a set day, and the bread and the cup taken in remembrance of Jesus. His mercies are new every morning, so let your thanks be new every morning too.

teen.open: Why does something amazing start to feel normal so fast? Because our eyes get used to it, not because it stopped being amazing. Yahweh gave His people ways to keep remembering.
teen.close: So why do miracles feel ordinary? We get used to them. The fix is to remember on purpose: write down what Yahweh has done, talk about it, and thank Him every morning.

senior.open: The title asks why past wonders come to feel ordinary. The Word answers that the eye adjusts, most of all in seasons of plenty, and it gives memorials so that what Yahweh did is asked about and told again.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. The works remain true; it is our seeing that fades. Remember by choice, tell the next generation, and keep the Lord's table, so that yesterday's gift is never treated as furniture.

ll330-he-healeth-the-broken-in-heart.reason: Works through the talk's claims point by point; the yes (Yahweh heals and binds, unites the heart, redeems rather than erases the past) is spread across nine sections; ends on weekly practices, not the answer.
ll330-he-healeth-the-broken-in-heart.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can a broken heart be made whole? Yes. The Word says the wound is real and heavy, and that Yahweh is near the broken in heart and binds up their wounds by hand (Psalms 147:3). He made the whole of you, spirit, soul and body. He unites a divided heart when you ask, restores the soul, and redeems the past instead of cutting it out. Healed is not the same as erased. Here is how the Word shows it.
ll330-he-healeth-the-broken-in-heart.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can a broken heart be made whole? Yes, by the One who made all of you. The wound is real, and your body may carry it, but Yahweh is near. You ask Him to unite your heart and search it; He gives a new one. He does not erase what happened. Joseph named the evil and the good Yahweh brought from it, and Jesus kept His scars and offered them to Thomas. Bring the memory to Him as it is, let others help bear it, see a skilled helper without shame, and ask Him to open your eyes. He restoreth the soul (Psalms 23:3).

teen.open: Can a heart that has been badly hurt be made whole? Yes. Yahweh is close to people who are hurting, and He heals broken hearts gently, one wound at a time.
teen.close: So can a broken heart be healed? Yes. Bring your hurt to Jesus just as it is, tell someone you trust, and let Him heal you. Healed does not mean forgotten; it means He made something good from it.

senior.open: The title asks whether a broken heart can be made whole. The Word answers yes: the wound is real, but Yahweh is nigh unto the broken in heart, binds up their wounds, and restores the soul.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. Yahweh does not erase the past; He redeems it, as He did for Joseph. Pour out your heart before Him, accept the help of others and of skilled physicians, and trust Him to make you whole.
